text: The first question wants what I told Marilla, with the picture of the tree in it. The second is about the scholarship, and why I went to bed with my cheeks tingling. The third asks you to look back over the whole week. That one’s the hardest, and the best. Look for what I say out loud, and what you can only see.

The top sentence is about me, and I wish it weren’t quite so true. Lonesomer. Isn’t that a lovely, sad word? Find the joining verb, and the word that compares. The bottom sentence needs a stop in the middle and two capitals, one of them mine. I’d be grateful if you gave it back. A girl’s name ought to stand up straight, even when she’s homesick.

Six sentences, each telling you what kind of verb something is, and some of them are fibbing, which I used to do about geometry. Only tap the fibs. The test is simple: put was where the verb is and see whether the sentence still makes sense. I used to think every verb was full of action. Most of mine were, I suppose.

This is the last day of word work this week, and two of the four ask you to catch a mistake. Here’s a secret I learned at the Entrance: some of the sentences are perfectly right, and tapping those costs you. So don’t tap because you’re nervous. Tap because you’re sure. I wish someone had told me that about geometry.

There’s a box here about knowing who you are. It sounds like something you’d find out all at once, like a fairy in a dell. It isn’t, I’ve discovered. It comes in little bits, and one of them came on Marilla’s lap, in the kitchen, in my new green dress. Read, and watch what I tell her. Then decide whether I was right.

Now the writing. I used to answer every question with three paragraphs and a poem. Miss Stacy taught me that the short way is stronger. So answer what’s asked, in plain words, and prove it with something from the book. If you quote me, quote me exactly. I chose those words very carefully, even the little ones.

Matching again: the two roots and the two little front parts. I adore roots. A word that means to look can grow into something grand to stare at, and a word that means to build can end up meaning to tear down, depending on what you put in front. Say a word you know aloud before you match. Then ask which part is doing the work.

This chapter has a leaving in it, and a lonely little room, and Josie Pye, which is a very odd mixture. There’s one stop, at the end. Before you get there, watch what I hold onto and what I let go. And watch the last page, because something happens there that makes everything feel enormous again. I won’t say what. I’m trying to be less dramatic.

Six comparing words, and some are made all wrong, with too many endings piled on, or more stuck in front of a word that already has an ending. I used to pile on extra words exactly like that, to sound grand. Now I try to say a thing once, properly. Tap only the ones that say it twice, or say it wrong.

There’s a little menu of ways to show what you know, and you only pick one. I would want to do all five, but I’m learning that choosing is a skill too. Pick the one you could do best, not the one that sounds grandest. I’ve learned that the hard way. Then use the words as if they were your own. They are, now.

Hello, it’s Anne, and today’s question is about me, which feels very strange to say out loud. Who am I really, when everything is changing? I’ll try not to make a speech of it. First there’s word work, and you’ll be hunting for mistakes. Then you read about the day I leave Green Gables. Then you decide what stays the same. I’m still deciding myself.

The box says a big idea has to hold up twice. I like that. It’s like trying on a dress in front of two different mirrors. So when you think you’ve found what this week is really about, take it back to another chapter and see if it still fits. If it doesn’t, it was only one page’s idea. Keep going until it fits both.

The last edit is your ears. Read your whole story out loud, slowly, the way you’d recite at a concert, and wherever you stumble, something is wrong. Fix it. Then say what you’re proud of. That part felt like boasting to me at first. It isn’t. Knowing what you did well is how you do it again.

The first question is about what I gave up and what I planned instead. The second is about Gilbert and the school, and the hill. The third is the whole book at once. For that one, you might begin at the station, where Matthew found me sitting on a pile of shingles, and end at the gate. Everything in between is yours to choose from.

The top sentence is Mrs. Lynde’s, and when she said it, I sprang straight to my feet. Find the helper and the word it helps. The bottom sentence is two sentences that ran together, which is exactly how I talked when I was eleven. Split it, and give everyone their capitals. Gilbert included. Especially Gilbert, just now.

A little paragraph about this chapter, and some of the sentences are missing a helper. Tap only those. Read each sentence out loud in your head. Your ear will catch a missing word before your eye does. Mine always has, even when my eyes were busy imagining something else entirely. Leave the good sentences alone.

The last word work of the book, and most of it asks you to catch mistakes. Some sentences are perfectly right, and tapping those costs you. So tap only when you’re sure. I spent years being sure about things I was wrong about. Gilbert, for one. So I’ve learned to look twice before I decide. You do the same.

There’s a box here about the bend in the road. When I left Queen’s, my future looked like a straight road, and I thought I could see a long way down it. Then it turned. I didn’t choose the turn. I only chose how to walk around it. Read, and watch two people give something up. Then decide whether either of us lost anything.

The writing now. The last question asks you to look back across the whole book, and that’s a great deal to hold at once. Don’t try to hold all of it. Pick one early moment and one late one, and set them side by side. Two good details are better than ten hurried ones. Miss Stacy taught me that, and she was right, as usual.

Matching again: the writing root, the throwing root, and two little pieces that go in front. I adore them, because they’re hiding in so many of the words I use. Before you match, say a word you know with that root in it. Then ask which piece is doing which job. It’s rather like working out who in a story is really doing the work.

One stop, at the very end, with what I said to Marilla about the bend. Before you get there, watch the kitchen when Marilla comes home from town. Watch who gives up what, and why. And watch the hill, near the end. Something happens there that I’d been waiting five years for, though I didn’t know I was waiting.

Six words, and some have their endings put on wrong. Tap only those. Look closely at the spot where the ending meets the word. That’s where every mistake in this list lives. I’m going to be a teacher now, you know, so I’ll be hunting for exactly this on a whole room of slates. Practice on these for me.

This one is a menu, and you only choose one thing from it. I would want to do all five, of course. But I’m about to give up something big, and I’ve found that choosing one thing and doing it well feels better than I expected. Pick the one you could do best. Then use the words as if they’d always been yours.

Hello, it’s Anne. Today’s question is about two people choosing love over ambition, and what that teaches. One of those people is me, so I may not be perfectly fair. First there’s word work, and some of it is catching mistakes. Then you read the last chapter. Then you look back over the whole road, all the way from the train station to the gate.

The box asks what changed in me, and what stayed exactly the same. I’ve thought about it a great deal, and I’m not the right person to judge. Nobody sees herself straight, not even in the best looking glass. So find one early moment and one late one, and set them side by side. Then decide for yourself. I’d honestly rather you did.

Your story is finished. Today you read it out loud to someone. Go slowly, and pause where it matters. I used to recite so fast that nobody could follow me. Then write a little about how your writing has grown, and how I’ve grown, too. Be specific. Specific is always better than splendid, even though splendid is such a lovely word.

The model sentence is mine, and I’m rather proud of it. Notice how my words are split in two, with my name tucked in the middle. The sentence you fix is simpler, but it uses the same pieces. A little word that should always stand tall appears twice. And the pause belongs inside the quotation marks, where it can keep the speaker company.

Word study! I do love words, especially long, grand ones. It’s the last day of the week, so you’ve met all of these words before. It’s rather like meeting old friends again, which I haven’t had much chance to do. Go quickly, but carefully. Marilla says carefully matters more, and I suppose she’s right, though I’d never tell her so.

Marilla is driving me to White Sands to see Mrs. Spencer, to sort out the mistake about the boy. I’m trying very hard not to think about what happens after that. So instead, listen to how I tell things in this chapter. Notice when I stop saying what happened and start saying what I imagined. I do that rather a lot, I’m afraid.

Well, now you know all about me. Bolingbroke, and Mrs. Thomas, and Mrs. Hammond with her three pairs of twins, and the asylum. It isn’t a very romantic history, is it? But I’d rather you didn’t feel too sorry for me. Now it’s your turn to write. Point to my words in the book when you answer. I said a great many of them, so you have plenty to choose from.

This chapter is mostly me talking, which I know won’t surprise you in the least. As you read, keep a list in your head of every home I mention, and who I lived with there. There are more than you’d think. When you reach the stopping point, you’ll be asked what kept me hopeful. Your list will help you answer truthfully. Don’t rush. It’s a long drive.

You get to choose how to show what you know, which is exactly the sort of thing I like. If a word still feels slippery, try explaining it to someone younger. That’s the quickest way to find out whether you really own it. Placid is the hardest one for me. I don’t believe I’ve been placid for a single minute of my life.

Hello! I’m Anne Shirley, Anne spelled with an e, and I’m guiding your lesson today, which is the most thrilling thing that’s happened to me in ages. Today’s question is how a person’s past shapes who they are. By the end, you’ll be able to explain how mine shaped me. We’ll finish off our plurals, too, and I promise to talk a little less than usual.

Here’s a test I think is perfectly delicious. Choose a moment you know well from these chapters, and imagine someone else telling it. Marilla would tell my story very plainly, I expect, with hardly an adjective in it. Today you’ll hear me tell it myself, so you can decide which parts are what happened and which parts are how I chose to say it.

Today you give your character a history, the way I gave Marilla mine. You only need three sentences. Where do they come from? What have they been through? And what do they want most in the whole world? That last one matters most. It’s the part that keeps a person going, and it will keep your story going too. Choose specific words, not boring ones.

[warmly] No headset today? That’s all right. We can take the trip from a window seat, with only our imaginations. That’s a very fine way to travel. Choose the name I gave each place, then lay out our drive in order, from the station all the way to Green Gables. [brightly] If you can see it in your mind, you’ve been there too.

[brightly] Oh, hello! It’s me, Anne. I’ve just had the most wonderful drive of my whole life, eight miles with Mr. Cuthbert. [dreamy] The people here give such plain names to such beautiful places, so I gave them better ones. Will you build our drive with me, stop by stop, in the very same order? Then tell me my new names out loud. It would give me such a thrill.

[gasps] You did it! You built the whole drive, and every stop is right where it belongs. I’ve pressed an apple blossom from the White Way of Delight, just for you. [softly] Keep it safe, so you’ll always remember our trip.

Word study! Today you produce the answers yourself, so there’s nowhere to hide, which I find rather thrilling and slightly alarming. Four word parts to type, three of this week’s words to fit into sentences, four feeling words, and four single letters. In every game, read the whole sentence before you type into its gap. A gap on its own will fool you every time. Check each box before you move on.

Two more days till the picnic, and I have thought of very little else, which Marilla says is setting my heart on things. This week’s watch is about finding out what you’ll trade to get what you want. I want that picnic more than anything. As you read, keep two lists in your head: what somebody wants, and what they give up for it. Then decide whether the trade was worth it.

Well, now you know the worst of me. Marilla thought I’d lost her brooch, and I hadn’t, and she shut me in my room until I confessed. So I confessed to something I never did, with a bridge in it. Then she found the brooch on her shawl, and I went to the picnic after all, and the ice cream was sublime. Now say what you noticed, and show it from the book.

Four words in the bank and only three gaps, so one gets left out, poor thing. Read each sentence to the end. Then ask what job the gap is doing. Is it describing a mouth, a feeling, or a temper? That narrows it wonderfully. Try your word in the sentence out loud. If it sounds foolish, it is. Leave the hardest gap for last and the bank will have done half your work.

Hello, it’s Anne Shirley, and I’m guiding you again, which is a great honor. Today’s question is how one bad choice grows into a bigger trouble, and you’re to follow the chain link by link. I know something about that, though I’d rather not say what yet. In word study you build the answers yourself instead of sorting them. And the reading move isn’t in the warm-up today. It’s waiting on the Reading tab.

Oh, a cover! It’s the most important page, because it’s the one everybody sees first, so it ought to say something true. When I was little I thought growing up meant everything turning grand. It doesn’t. You get pruned down and branched out. Write your sentence so it’s true for anyone, not only me. That’s the hard part. It’s also the best part.

One sentence, said three ways. Anne can say a thing six ways before she gets to the end of the lane, and I used to think that was showing off. It isn’t. It’s trying them on. Read the sentence, find the doing word, and change just that first. Then start it somewhere else. Then add where or how. Keep the one that sounds most like you.

Sorting doing words. Gertie Pye squeaks her pencil through every grammar lesson and it makes my blood run cold, so I’d rather do it here. Say each chip with its little word in front, the she or the they. Listen to the end of the doing word. Some change, some don’t, and some have a helper word stuck on the front. That’s your three groups. Name them in your own words.

Four boxes. Word parts to type, then words to guess and match, then two sorts. I like sorts, because you can tell when you’re finished. Do them in order, and read every bit of a box before you tap anything, because two of them have a third column, and the third column is the tricky one. Anne would say the tricky one is the interesting one. Anne isn’t doing your sorting.

I’m dressed and I’m nervous, which is a silly thing to be about tea. The box on courage says it’s doing the hard thing while you’re still frightened. I’d have said courage was not being frightened. So while you read, watch for somebody who’s scared and goes anyway. And watch what fear looks like from the outside. Mostly it looks like standing very still.

Well. Now you know. I was awfully sick, I had a headache all the next day, and Mother smelled my breath and that was that. She says Anne did it on purpose. I don’t believe it for one minute. Anne didn’t have any herself, she said she didn’t want any after the apples. But nobody’s asking me. They’re asking you, so show it from the book, not from how you feel.

It’s Diana again. The question at the top is about an honest mistake turning into a real problem. I don’t know anything about that. All I know is I’m going to tea, and I’m awfully excited. So as you go, keep two lists in your head: what somebody meant to do, and what actually happened. Then there are doing words to sort, and a c-and-g rule that isn’t as simple as it looks.

Mother and I can watch the same thing and come away with two different stories. It used to make me cross. Now I think it’s just how people are. So when the box says pick one event, pick a small one, and put each person beside it. Then find the one thing somebody didn’t know. That’s usually the whole gap, right there. It was for Mother and me, anyway.

The first question is about the tea, and it wants two details, not one. Look at what Mrs. Allan invites Anne to do. The second is about the roof. Look at who dared whom first, and then at what Anne says up there. The third is about Marilla. I didn’t see her face. I was looking at Anne. Find the line that tells you what hit Marilla. It’s a strong one.

The top sentence is Anne’s, word for word, and it’s awfully grand. Look at everything it does. The marks around her words, my name tucked in between commas, the period inside at the very end. The bottom one is two thoughts squashed together, one already done and one not yet. Give them each a sentence of their own. A stop, then a capital. And Anne’s name wants its capital too.

One long sentence, and lots of doing words in it. Some are already done and some haven’t happened yet. Tap every one that isn’t happening right now. There’s more than one, so keep going after the first. Read it slowly, a word at a time, and ask of each one, is this now? If it isn’t, tap it. Anne reads too fast. I read slowly, and I get things right.

Four bits of word work. Two you’ve seen before, so you’ll be quick. One asks you to tap every doing word that isn’t happening right now, and there’s more than one, so don’t stop at the first. The other asks for words that kept their y when you’d think it would change. Those are the sneaky ones. Ruby Gillis would tap everything in sight. Don’t be Ruby.

There’s a box here about being brave and being dared. I’ll tell you about daring, because everybody in Avonlea is doing it this summer. Somebody says you can’t, and then you simply have to. The boys started it, and now it’s us. It’s mostly silly things, climbing trees and hopping round gardens. Watch whether Anne picks the dare, or the dare picks Anne. I’m only saying watch.

Oh, Anne. I begged her not to. I told her it wasn’t fair to dare anybody to do anything so dangerous. She had an answer ready, of course. She always does. When she fell I truly thought she was killed. She wasn’t. Now you write about it. Use what people said, the actual words, not what you think they meant. And don’t forget the tea. That was the nice part.

Matching today. Two little word parts, and two word roots that go with them. One part means against. One means away, or down. The roots are the rest of words you already know. Say the whole word out loud, then take it apart. If you get stuck, think of coming down the stairs, or going away from home. Those two will tell you a great deal.

One stop, after the tea. Anne gets a letter with Miss on the front, and she can’t stop talking about it. Think about why one little word could matter so much to her. Then read on into my party. Watch the garden, and watch who dares whom, and in what order. The order matters more than you’d think. That’s all I’m going to say. Truly.

That sentence is Anne coming up the lane with her letter, and it’s exactly how she moves when she’s happy. Like a sprite the wind is blowing about. The book doesn’t say she went fast. It says dancing, and then it gives you the sunshine and the shadows. When you write yours, choose the moving word first. Then the comparison. Then two things the place looks like.

These words all ended in y once. Most changed it to an i when something got added. You don’t want those. You want the ones that kept their y when you might have expected it to change. So for each word, look at the letter in front of where the y was, and look at what got added. The y had a reason to stay. Find the ones with a reason.

These are the same four words as yesterday. Now you match them without the cards, and that’s the real test. Don’t just pick what sounds nice. Say each word in a sentence about someone you know. If it fits the person, you’ve likely got it. I said kindred about Anne and it fitted perfectly. Then I said it about Josie Pye. It did not.

Hello, it’s Diana. The question’s about pride, and how it makes people do dangerous things. I’ve known Anne a whole year now, and I’ll tell you, she has an awful lot of it. Today there’s a tea, and then there’s a party, and the party is at my house. Before all that there’s word work, and some sentences with more than one doing word in them. Find every one.

The box says every place lets you do some things and stops you doing others. That’s ever so true. At the manse Anne has to sit up straight and mind her manners. In our garden nobody’s minding anything. So as you read, keep asking what each place lets Anne do, and what it won’t. I know which place I’d rather be. I’m not sure Anne does.

This part is like the roof. Your kid wants something and is afraid of something, both at once, and everybody’s watching. Write it so the reader feels both. Then stop, right before your kid decides. Don’t tell what happens next. I couldn’t breathe, standing in our garden, not knowing. That’s what keeps a reader reading. Leave them standing in the garden too.

The first question asks what the club is called and what each of us has to do. Anne made the rules, so look at what she tells Marilla. The second wants Anne’s story in two sentences. Two! I heard every word of it, and I couldn’t. Keep the people and the ending. The third asks why a moral matters to her. Look at who she says agrees.

That sentence is about me, and it’s quite true. I did write to Aunt Josephine about our club. Now say it three ways. Change the doing word first, but keep it about a letter. Then start the sentence somewhere else, with a when or a where. Then tell how I wrote it. Anne says one sentence said three ways is three times as good. I only half believe her.

The top sentence is Anne’s, and it’s about Matthew, who likes every story she writes. Look at the two doing words that tell what already happened. Neither one takes the usual ending. The bottom sentence is about me, I’m afraid, and somebody forgot my capital. There’s also a story that belongs to someone, and a sentence that never stops. Mend all three.

All of these doing words are already in the past, and not one of them takes the usual ending. But they break the rule in three different ways. Say each pair out loud, the now word and then the past one. Listen for how much changes. A little, a lot, or nothing at all. Anne says breaking a rule beautifully is half the fun. Here it’s the whole lesson.

Four bits of word work, and two of them sort into three columns, not two. That’s harder than it sounds. Ruby would put everything in the middle and hope. Don’t do that. Say each word out loud before you move it, because your ear knows more than you think. And the fill-ins want the back half of each word, not the front. Read the meaning first.

There’s a box here about learning from your mistakes. I know a little about that. Anne and I made up the Haunted Wood together, and we frightened ourselves so badly that neither of us would go through it after dark. Anne said she’d be contented with commonplace places after that. As you read, watch whether she is. I’m not sure she is.

Now you write, and it’s your answers, not your stories. Anne writes three pages when one line would do. Don’t. When a question asks what happened, say it plainly, then show me where in the book. When it asks why, give a reason and a line to back it up. And keep your summary short. Short is hard. I know, because Anne never manages it.

Two old roots today, living inside words you already use. One means to carry. The other means to pull, or to draw. The front of each word is already there, and you type the rest. Read the meaning after the blank first. Then ask, is something being carried here, or pulled? Think of a wagon, then a magnet. Anne would think of a chariot and a lodestone. A wagon does just as well.

Two stops. The first comes when Anne tells how each girl in the club writes. One of them is me, and I’ll say no more. Think about why four friends would make up such different stories. The second comes at the very end. Ask yourself why none of us ever writes about Avonlea. It’s right outside the window, and nobody thinks of it at all.

These words all end in a quiet e, and then something gets added. Sometimes the e stays and sometimes it goes. Look at the first letter of what’s been added, and look at what comes just before the e. Those two together decide it. One column is for words that never had the tricky sound at all. You’ll know them when you say them.

Four new words, and each card has a real sentence from the book above it. Some of them will sound strange to you. They sounded strange to me too, the first time. Use the sentence anyway, then look for word parts, then guess before you flip. Anne flips first and thinks afterward. I’d think first. Then tap.

Hello, it’s Diana. Today is about our story club, and how Anne works out what she thinks a good story is. She has a great many ideas about it. Before the reading there’s word work, doing words that don’t follow the usual rule for the past, and a spelling rule about a quiet letter e. Then you’ll tell the chapter in a few sentences. Just a few. Anne would need fifty.

The box says to tell a chapter in three sentences, not thirty. I’m rather good at that, because I never know what to do with my people, so I simply stop. Anne is the opposite. She keeps every lovely word and every sigh. So as you read, stop now and then and ask what has changed. If nothing has, that part can go.

Today you add. Find one place in your story where things happen too fast, where somebody falls or wins or cries and we never feel it. Then slow down and put in what we’d see or hear or feel. Anne’s stories are full of things happening, horses running away and people drowning. The part I love best is always the little bit in between. Put a little bit in.

The first question is about the very words I said when I burst in, so do look at them closely. I was rather out of breath. The second asks about Anne’s other reason for working so hard, the nobler one. The third is about Matthew. He hardly ever says anything, so when he does, it’s worth listening to.

Anne said the top sentence the minute she got home from town, and I agree with every word, except perhaps for Orchard Slope. Find the joining word, and the two that mean the very most. The bottom sentence has two names wanting capitals, and two thoughts squeezed together with nothing between them. Give them each a little room.

Two sentences, and the joining verbs are hiding in with the doing ones, the way I hide behind Anne when Josie Pye comes along. There’s more than one. I always find the first and go skipping off, and then I have to come back. Ask of each verb, could I watch somebody do it? If not, try putting was in its place and see if the sentence still holds.

Four bits of word work, and two of them are tapping games with more than one right answer hiding. Don’t stop at the first one you find. That’s what I always do, and then I miss the rest and have to start over. Take each sentence one word at a time. Miss Stacy says slow and careful wins, and she’s generally right.

There’s a box here about who you want to tell first when something good happens. I know who Anne told, because I was there, running behind her across the yard. I never once thought she’d do anything else. I’d have done the very same thing, only with more shrieking. Read, and watch where her feet take her.

Now the writing part. I always want to put everything in, every lovely little thing, and Miss Stacy always crosses most of it out. Answer just what the question asks, and show where in the chapter you found it. If you use somebody’s exact words, put them in quotation marks. Then read it over once before you say it’s finished.

A matching game with yesterday’s two roots and two new little front parts. I always mix up the one that means in with the one that means down or away. So I say a real word out loud first, one I know, and listen to what it means. Try it. It’s ever so much easier than staring.

Most of this chapter is waiting, and Anne’s letter to me from town, which I’ve read at least eleven times. Notice how frightened she is, and how she still manages to cheer up Moody Spurgeon. Then the pass list. There’s one stop, at the end. Before you get there, keep asking why she wanted it so badly. It wasn’t only Gilbert.

That sentence is my favorite in the whole chapter. Look how it names two people and then goes back for one of them, as if it couldn’t help it. That little dash is doing such a lot. When you write yours, name two people, then pick one out on purpose. Your reader will know at once who matters most.

This one’s a bit of a trick. Most of the comparing words are right, and you’re only to tap the ones that are made wrong. Say each one out loud. If it sounds like something a very little child would say, it probably is wrong. Count the beats in the plain word, too. That always tells.

The same four words as yesterday, but no cards this time, so it’s all up to you. If you get stuck, picture somebody you know who fits the meaning. Jane Andrews fits one of them perfectly. Nothing rattles her. If nobody you know fits, try another meaning. It’s like choosing a dress, really.

Hello, it’s Diana! This is the chapter where the pass list comes out, and I simply can’t keep still. The question is whose pride matters most to Anne when she sees her name. First there’s word work: find the verbs that only join, and the comparing words that went wrong. Then read it for yourself. I promised I wouldn’t spoil it, and I won’t. Nearly.

The box says one word isn’t enough, and I think that’s perfectly fair. If somebody asked me what this chapter is about, I’d say success and be done. But that’s only the topic. What does the chapter say success is for? Watch who Anne thinks of first. I know who I’d run to. I ran to Anne, didn’t I?

Dialogue today, which is my favorite part of anybody’s story. Read every line out loud, the way I read Anne’s letter. Quotation marks around the words people say, a comma before the part that tells who said it, and a capital to start. If a line sounds like nobody would ever say it, change the words too, not just the marks.

The first question is about something she said to Mother when we met, and I was sitting right there. Why would a person use such big words at a moment like that? For the second, look at the ceremony, not just the promise. Who set it up, and why so grand? The third is about something Marilla said to her at home. I wasn’t there. Read it carefully and decide whether Marilla is right.

Word study! First there are word parts to match, and one of the four isn’t a front part at all, so read the meanings carefully. Then the same four words as yesterday, then a sentence to tap, then a row of words to say out loud. Saying words out loud helps more than you’d think. Do the four boxes in order, and don’t rush the last one because it looks easy.

I’m at home with a book, which is where I usually am. Mother thinks I read too much, and Father keeps giving me more. This week’s watch is about letting yourself look forward to things. I’m good at that. I’m not so good at the waiting. As you read, notice what somebody lets herself hope for, and how she behaves while she waits. Waiting badly and waiting well look very different.

So now you know. She asked me straight out if I could like her enough to be her bosom friend, and I said I guessed so. Then we joined hands over the garden path, pretending it was a stream, and swore. I got the giggles, but I meant it. And I’ve been explaining ice cream to her, which is harder than it sounds. Go on. Say what you noticed, and show it from the book.

Hello, it’s Diana Barry, and I’m your guide today, for the first time. Your question is about how a friendship starts, and you won’t find it in speeches. You’ll find it in small things people do, mostly with their hands. So watch hands. In word study you’ll be finding the words for things you can’t pick up. And there’s a poem to learn by heart. Say it out loud, not in your head.

This one’s like a game, and I love games. Pick something small that happens, the smaller the better. Then keep asking, and then what? Follow it in your head. When the chain seems to run out, push once more, because the last link is usually somebody who wasn’t even there when it started. If you can follow it all the way to what somebody is hoping for by the end, you’ve done it.

Oh, I could pick so many! The raspberry cordial, when Mother wouldn’t let me see her. Or the night Minnie May had croup and Anne knew exactly what to do. Mother forgave everything after that. Anne was so brave, and she never once bragged about it. Whatever you choose, pick an ink that matches how she felt. Anne would say that’s the most romantic part.

The first question is about Anne’s dress and her beads, next to all those city jewels. The second asks what she sees from the stage, and wants you to quote it. I’ll admit I’m curious what you’ll say about that one. The third is about the drive home, where Jane wants diamonds and Anne doesn’t.

The top sentence is from the book, and from where I sat, it was awful true. Find the joining verb, and what it joins Anne to. The bottom one is two sentences that ran into each other. Split them, and give everybody their capitals, Anne included. She’d want hers. She’s particular about that sort of thing, and about how her name is spelled.

Four blanks and four joining verbs, and each one gets used once. They’re close cousins, so try every choice in every blank and listen hard. Read the whole sentence, not just the words around the gap. Sometimes the end of it settles the matter, like a but halfway through that changes everything.

Four pieces of word work, and most of them ask you to build something instead of just picking. That’s harder, but it’s the kind of hard that sticks. If a blank stumps you, say the whole sentence out loud. Your ear knows more than you think. Mine has gotten me out of a few tight spots at the blackboard, anyhow.

There’s a box here about deciding what counts as rich. I wasn’t in the buggy going home, so I can’t tell you what was said there. But I saw that hotel, all lit up and dripping with diamonds, and I saw Anne in a plain white dress. Read, and watch what she decides is worth counting. I’d bet it isn’t the diamonds.

Now you write. Here’s how I’d go about it. Read the question twice, then find the spot in the chapter where the answer lives before you write a word. When a question asks for an exact moment, quote it. If you’re guessing why someone did something, say what in the book made you guess. Anne calls that being dull. I call it being right.

These blanks are all over the place: in the middle of a word, at the end, even at the very front. So read the whole line before you type. Most of them ask whether the word is about looking or about building. A crowd at a ball game is doing one of those. A barn raising is doing the other. The odd one out wants the ending for a person who does it.

Two stops. The first comes when Anne is up on that platform and can’t get a word out. Think about what changes for her, and what gets her started. The second stop comes on the drive home, after the concert. Listen to what she says she’s rich in, and ask whether she means it. I think she does. Honest.

I like this sentence because Anne doesn’t argue. She just says it, flat out, and then backs it up with three things nobody can take away from her. Look at the one word that tells you how she said it. Take that away and she sounds like she’s guessing. When you write yours, choose your how-word carefully. Then give three reasons. Three’s a strong number.

Four comparing words to build, and two decisions every time: how many beats the plain word has, and whether there’s a y at the end that needs changing first. Do them in that order. Anne and I have spelled each other down more times than I can count. Whoever checks the second thing usually wins.

Three sentences, three blanks, and four words in the bank, so one gets left over. Read each sentence all the way through before you choose; the end of a sentence usually tells you more than the start. I’ll own up that one of these words fits me pretty well. I won’t say which. Anne would say it was the wrong one.

Hi, it’s Gilbert. Today’s question is about one small moment at a concert, and what it shows about how Anne has grown. I was in the room for that moment, as it happens. First, some word work: building comparing words and filling in joining verbs. Then read the chapter, and decide for yourself what happened on that stage. I’ve got my own idea.

The box says some big ideas are never said out loud. That’s true at concerts, too. Nobody stands up and tells you what a moment meant; you have to work it out. So watch what Anne chooses, and what happens right after. Then write the sentence nobody in the chapter says. Don’t look to me for it. I was only smiling.

Read slowly today, slower than feels right. You’re hunting three things: the wrong word that sounds like the right one, a spelling you wouldn’t bet a nickel on, and a sentence that ought to be two. When I’m not sure of a word, I look it up. There’s no shame in that. The shame is leaving it wrong when you could have checked.

The first question is about Ruby and me, and what Anne wishes she had instead. Don’t ask me; I didn’t know. The second wants you to set the slate day beside this winter, and to quote the book. The third is about her dreaming at the window. Use what the book says she sees, not what you guess she sees.

Here’s a plain sentence about where Anne spent her spare hours this winter. Say it three ways: give it a new opener, swap the doing word, then add a where or a how. Anne used to crowd every fine big word she knew into a composition. Miss Stacy taught us both to say a thing plainly first. Try all three, then keep the one that tells the most. It usually has the best verb.

The top sentence is three words long, and it’s Jane Andrews talking about exams. I’ll admit I felt the same way. Find the little helper word, and the word it’s helping. The bottom one is two sentences crammed together, the way people talk when they’re nervous. Pull them apart and give them their capitals. Getting the small things right is half of any exam.

Some verbs come in pieces: a helper out front, and the word that carries the meaning at the end. Sometimes the helpers stack up two deep. Sometimes there’s no helper at all. For each one, ask which word is doing the real work and which ones are only standing beside it. Then count the ones standing beside it. That count is your group.

Four pieces of word work, and two of them ask you to sort into three groups instead of two. Don’t rush the third group. That’s where the thinking is. At Queen’s, the professors don’t much care whether you guessed right. They want to know how you knew. So for every one you place, be ready to say why. It’s a good habit, and a hard one.

There’s a box here about a rivalry without bitterness. I can only tell you my half. For years Anne wouldn’t look at me, and this winter she still doesn’t. We haven’t said a word since the pond. But racing her feels different now, at least on my side. It feels like racing someone, not fighting them. Read, and see what she wants out of it now. I’d like to know myself.

Now you write. Here’s a trick from exam week. Read the question twice, and the second time look for the trap. Then find the line in the chapter before you write a word. If a question asks for a quote, copy the words exactly, commas and all. The professors notice, and so will your teacher. Anne thinks checking is cheating. It isn’t. It’s checking.

Two old roots today. One means to write, and one means to throw. They don’t stand on their own; they hide inside longer words, and you have to dig them out. When a blank stumps you, ask what the word is doing. Is somebody putting words on paper, or sending something flying? That tells you which root belongs. It works on Latin, too, I’m finding.

Two stops. The first comes when the girls are fretting about exams and Anne says something about trying and failing. Ask yourself whether she means it. The second stop comes at the very end, when she’s looking out a window. Watch what she’s dreaming about. I wasn’t there for either of those, so you’ll know more than I do. That doesn’t happen to me often.

These are mistakes from real drafts, and three different rules got broken. Before you sort, say each word with its ending, then picture how it should look on the page. All three rules wake up at the same moment: when an ending meets a base word. I lost a spelling match at Avonlea school on exactly that moment once. Anne didn’t let me forget it.

Four new words, and each one has its sentence from the book sitting right on top. Read that sentence first, then take the word apart, then check. One of these words fits a girl I know rather too well. I won’t say which, or she’d prove it on the spot. The matching game at the end is quick. Don’t let quick turn into careless.

Hi, it’s Gilbert. Today’s question is about winning, and how wanting to win can change. I know a bit about that. I’ve been racing Anne Shirley since our first term in Avonlea school. First, some word work: two old roots, and verbs that come in pieces. Then the chapter, our winter at Queen’s. Watch what Anne wants now. It isn’t what it used to be.

The box asks you to hold two Annes side by side: the girl who came to Avonlea and the young lady at Queen’s. I can help with the first one. She once broke a slate over my head. This winter she still won’t say a word to me, and I don’t say one to her. That isn’t the whole change, and it isn’t mine to explain. Find it in what she says and does.

Publishing starts with the ending. I like that. An ending is where a reader decides what the whole story meant. Your rough last scene has been waiting a long time. Today you replace it, using one move. Pick the move that fits your character, not the one that sounds fanciest. Then read your first line and your last line together. They should sound like they know each other.

The first question is why it hit her so hard, and I’m the wrong person to ask. Look back at what somebody else called her earlier in the book, and what she did then. The second is about a punishment. Think what sitting next to me meant after what I’d done. Not to me. To her. The third goes back over the whole week. Pick one chain, and make each link touch the next.

First day back, and I mean to make an impression. This week’s watch is friendship, and I’ll tell you what I know about it: you find out who your friends are after you’ve made a fool of yourself. As you read, watch who stands by whom when things go wrong, and what it costs them. And watch me. I’m not saying I’ll behave. I’m saying watch.

Right. So I called her Carrots, holding up her braid, and she cracked her slate over my head. I told Mr. Phillips it was my fault, which it was. I said sorry after, honest, and she walked past like I wasn’t there. Then I gave her a candy heart and she ground it underfoot. I don’t know why it landed so hard. You’ve read more of her than I have. Tell me.

Five choices and you only do one, so don’t pick the easy one. Pick the one you’d actually enjoy. If you like arguing, teach a word to a younger kid; you’ll find out fast whether you really know it. If you like the book, hunt the chapter for a word close to one of ours. Whatever you choose, use the word the way the book does. Read your answer back once before you move on.

Hello. Gilbert Blythe here, and it’s my first go at guiding, so go easy on me. Your question is about a moment in the schoolroom where somebody does something sudden, and what was inside her that made her do it. I’ll be honest, I don’t know what’s coming any better than you do. In word study you’re checking a draft somebody else wrote, so you get to be the teacher for once. Enjoy that.

Today you write five scenes, one line each. Look at what the author did with me. The whole slate business is one scene, one room, told all the way through, and it’s the only thing anybody will remember about this chapter. So when you write your five lines, don’t cram. Each scene gets one place and one thing that happens. And make the worst moment a choice somebody makes, not just bad luck.

I’ll own up. One of Anne’s turning points was me, calling her Carrots. She cracked a slate over my head, and she wouldn’t speak to me for years. Then one evening she stopped me on the road and held out her hand. If you pick the slate, go easy on me. If you don’t, find something that shows how she got from that slate to that road.

The first question mentions a brooch. I know nothing of any brooch. Look back to the chapter where it happened and put that girl beside the one at my door. The second is about what she asked me to do, and I was there. Look at what I said just after she asked it. The third is about Diana. Diana stayed in the kitchen. I heard her through the door, once. Ask why she stayed.

The sentence you are to mend has me in it, spelled without a single capital letter. I never. The top sentence shows you how it ought to go: a name with its capital, a full stop at the end. The bottom one is two thoughts run together. Find where the first one ends and put a period there. Then the capitals. Every name gets one, and mine has two parts, so it gets two.

She stood in my doorway, white as paper, and said she had come to confess. I meant to be cross for a month. I lasted about four minutes. I have unpacked my valise and told them I am staying, simply to get better acquainted with that Anne-girl. Now you are to say what you noticed. Say what you saw her do, not what you felt. Evidence, hey? I would ask it of a witness.

Josephine Barry. I am told I am to be your guide, and I have never guided anything but a knitting needle. I have read the question. Two girls, it says, jump into a bed with an old woman asleep in it. I am the old woman. I have not read what comes next and am not looking forward to it. You are to watch what the girl does afterward. So am I.

What that child thought as she stood at my door I can only guess. What she said, I heard. Your second scene wants the thing nobody hears, one line of thinking inside your kid’s head. Sam’s boy thinks three words, three times over. When I was young we thought in longer sentences. Yours needn’t be long. It need only be true. Then the wall, whatever it is, comes into view.

The first question asks for two things the girls did in town. I took them to most of them, so choose well. The second asks why the concert moved Anne so. She told me she did not see how she could ever go back to common life. I suggested ice cream. The third asks what she decided about town and country. Use her words, not mine.

The top sentence is about me, and quite right too. I did keep them there all day. Count the capitals in it. A day of the week, a title, a name, and a show grand enough to deserve one. The bottom sentence is about the concert, and it has run two thoughts together, as young people do. Put a stop between them. And give the girl her capital.

Four sentences, told as though they were happening now. Put each doing word into the past, where it belongs. None of them takes the usual ending, so do not try. Say yesterday in front of it, and listen. Your ear will tell you, if you let it. Then the box at the end asks for two sentences of your own about this chapter. Make them good ones.

Building, today. You type every answer yourself, and there is nothing to choose from. A missing root, a missing word, a doing word put into the past, and a piece added onto the end. When I was young we did this sort of thing on a slate with no help whatever. You have a box that checks your work. Say each one aloud first. Then type it.

There is a box here about learning from one’s mistakes. I have made a few myself, though I seldom admit it. Once I was very angry with two little girls for jumping on my bed. I meant to go home the very next day. Then one of them came to confess, and I unpacked. Watch for the moment Anne is glad about something she would once have sulked over. I was there, and I noticed.

Now you write, and I shall be particular. Say what happened plainly. If you are asked why, give a reason, and point to the line in the book that proves it. Do not decorate. I have read a great many stories by Avonlea girls, and the decoration was never the best part. The best part was always the one true thing in the middle.

Four words, and each has lost its back half. The front is there, and the meaning is there, so you are not entirely abandoned. Read each meaning slowly. Then ask yourself one question. Is something being carried here, or is something being pulled? There are only two roots to choose from. At my time of life, I find most questions come down to two choices.

Two stops. The first comes when Anne gives her verdict on town life. I laughed, I am afraid. Think about what her answer tells you about her. The second comes at the very end, after she has left my house. I was not there for it, so you must tell me. Which part do you think she will remember longest?

I was not in that lane, of course. I do not keep cows. But that sentence tells me more about the Anne-girl than an hour of her conversation. The cows plod along. She dreams. And her head is full of a battle. Three things, and not one word about the weather. When you write yours, choose your three as carefully, and leave the sunset out.

Four words, and a piece to add to each. Two rules at once. First, does the word end with a soft sound before its quiet e? Then, what letter does the new piece begin with? Both answers decide whether the e stays. Write each one out in full before you check. Carelessness in spelling is like carelessness in anything. It shows.

Three sentences, three blanks, and four words to choose from. One word is left over, which is perfectly in order. Read each sentence to the end before you choose. Then say it aloud with your word in the blank. If it sounds like something a sensible person would say, keep it. If it sounds like nonsense, I dare say it is.

Josephine Barry. I have had two girls from Avonlea in my house this week, which is two more than usual. Your question asks what Anne discovers about herself in town. I asked her very nearly the same thing myself, and she made me wait for the answer. First, some word work, where you build the words yourself. Then the chapter. Then three sentences. Not four.

The box says most chapters lean on one moment. Find it, and the rest falls into place. Anne will tell you a great deal about horses, and balloons, and ice cream at eleven o’clock at night. Not all of it matters equally. As you read, ask which moment the chapter would collapse without. I know which one I would choose. Whether she would choose the same, I cannot say.

Today you swap. A dull doing word for a lively one. A line anybody might say for one only that person would say. And one small action that belongs to your character and nobody else. The Anne-girl kissed my wrinkled cheek on the veranda. Nobody else would have dared. Diana certainly did not. That is the sort of small thing that tells you exactly who someone is.

Freedom Watch. On my tours, I’d stop people at the edge of a marsh and ask them to just look for one minute. Most people noticed more in that minute than on the whole walk. Harriet can’t leave the house where she works, but she can look. Watch what she sees through the window, and what it makes her wonder. Sometimes freedom starts that small.

Chapter 1 opens on a spring day that’s beautiful outside and full of work inside. Keep track of what Harriet does, what she eats, and where her eyes go when nobody is watching her. Near the end, something goes badly wrong. Notice who comes looking for her, and the question she asks him. I underlined that question in my own copy.

Hey, I’m Marcus. I grew up on Maryland’s Eastern Shore, near the Choptank River, and last summer I led walking tours on the same roads Harriet Tubman knew as a girl. This year I’m writing my first research paper about her, so we’re learning together. Today you’ll read Chapter 1. Here’s the question: what does one ordinary day tell us about Harriet’s life, and about what she dreams of?

Today’s Freedom Watch is about small rebellions. Harriet can’t escape, and she can’t fight back. But there’s one thing she will not do, no matter who asks her, not even her own mother. Watch for it. This chapter has a hard part in it, so take it slowly. Then ask yourself: is saying no quietly still a kind of freedom? And what does it cost her?

Chapter 2 starts in the cabin where Harriet’s family lives. Pay attention to the cabin itself: the fireplace, the beds, and one thing her mother made by hand. Then listen to what her mother and her father each say about smiling. They don’t agree. Watch where Harriet stands. That handmade thing shows up in your word game, too.

Hey, it’s Marcus. Chapter 1 ended with Harriet in a peck of trouble, and Chapter 2 is named for it. When I started my research, I thought her story would begin with an escape. It doesn’t. It begins with a girl who won’t give in, even in small ways. Today’s question: what kind of trouble is Harriet in, and what does it tell us about her?

Freedom Watch: learning what you’re not supposed to know. In Harriet’s time, the law tried to keep enslaved people from learning to read. But learning found other ways in: stories, songs, and news passed from cabin to cabin. On my tours, people were always surprised how fast news traveled without a single phone. Watch how much Harriet learns without a book.

There’s no schoolhouse in Chapter 3, but there are teachers everywhere. Notice the old man who can read, and what he reads aloud. Notice the songs, and what they might really mean. Then notice the walks in the woods near the end. I’ve walked woods like those. What is Harriet learning there that no book could teach her?

Hey, it’s Marcus. Harriet never went to school, not for a single day. So how did she learn so much? That’s what Chapter 3 is about. Sterling calls it School Days, and I think she means it with a little bit of a smile. Keep a tally of every teacher Harriet has. Today’s question: what does school mean for an enslaved child in Maryland?

Freedom Watch: hearing the whistle. Before anyone can go somewhere new, they have to hear that it’s there. Listen for the stories Harriet hears in this chapter, and who tells them. Notice what happens inside her while she listens, even though she doesn’t say a word. Then think about a story you once heard that changed what you thought was possible.

In Chapter 4, Harriet meets Jim, who has already tried to run away twice. Listen to his stories about the steam train, and about another railroad with very unusual conductors. Watch for the song the workers sing in the barn. The chapter ends suddenly, with a hard choice and a frightening moment. Take a breath there, and watch what Harriet decides.

Hey, it’s Marcus. Harriet is fifteen now, and stronger than most of the grown men she works beside. In Chapter 4 she meets someone who has already run away twice, and she starts hearing about trains, the real kind and another kind. Today’s question: what does a train mean to Harriet? Here’s a hint: it isn’t only about riding.

Freedom Watch: the strength nobody planned for. Master and the men who come to look at Harriet only see her worth in dollars. But during the long months in the cabin, something changes inside her that nobody can measure. In my research, this is the part I keep coming back to. Watch for the moment Sterling tells you how Harriet sees herself now.

Chapter 5 covers a lot of time, so watch the time words: holidays, seasons, even a year. Track how Harriet’s strength comes back, one step at a time. Notice where she keeps her money, and count it as it grows. Later you’ll meet someone new on the courthouse steps in Cambridge. I’ve walked those Cambridge streets. Read that part closely.

Hey, it’s Marcus. Chapter 4 ended with Harriet badly hurt, struck by an iron weight that was meant for a runaway. Chapter 5 is called Not Worth a Sixpence. When I first read that title, it made me angry, because somebody says those words about Harriet. Today’s question: what do they miss about her? And who is she becoming while nobody is paying attention?

Freedom Watch: the moment of decision. On my tours, people asked me when Harriet made up her mind. I used to say it was one big moment. Now that I’ve read more, I’m not so sure. In this chapter, watch for every time she has a reason to stop, and what she does instead. The road she knows isn’t safe. The road north is a mystery. Which is scarier?

Before you open Chapter 6, get your sequence notes ready. This chapter moves fast, and the order matters. Watch the Quaker lady, and how carefully Harriet speaks to her. Listen for the words thee and thy; that’s how Quakers talked. Keep an eye on what Harriet carries, and on one thing she gives away. Listen for a song, too. Sterling prints every word of it.

Hey, it’s Marcus. Chapter 5 ended with Master’s death, and with Harriet saying it out loud to John, one slow word at a time: I’m going to run away. He told her she’d never make it. In my research notes, Chapter 6 gets a whole page of its own. Today’s question: what does it take to step off the plantation, alone, toward a North you’ve never seen?

Freedom Watch: the help of strangers. Harriet walks this whole chapter by herself, but she isn’t really alone. Some of her helpers aren’t even there. They gave her directions, or taught her something years ago. Others she meets for the very first time. In my research, I keep finding the same thing: almost every escape had helpers along the way. Count every one you find.

Chapter 7 is one long journey, so keep a clock in your head. The moon, the sun, and the stars all tell you the time. I grew up near the Choptank, and it changes as you follow it upstream. Notice how it changes for Harriet, and why she walks in the water. Near the end, watch what she decides at a dark house.

Hey, it’s Marcus. At the end of Chapter 6, Harriet left her quilt on the Quaker lady’s doorstep and walked away singing. Now she’s on her own. In Chapter 7, the North Star is her guide. But a star only shines at night. Today’s question: when daylight comes and the star is gone, how does Harriet still find her way north?

Freedom Watch: free, but not yet whole. Harriet has dreamed about crossing the line to freedom for a long time. Watch what she finds when she gets there, and who is around her. When I go back to the Choptank, I always think about the people who never got to leave. So ask yourself: can freedom feel complete while the people you love are still waiting?

Two chapters today, so keep a running list of stops as you go. Watch the clothes Harriet wears from place to place, because each outfit has a job to do. Look for a room that isn’t where you’d expect it. In Chapter 9, notice the moments when her mind goes back home. And listen closely to the man she meets near the end.

Hey, it’s Marcus. Last time, Harriet handed a Quaker woman a note and got a broom back. Today we read two chapters, and they carry her a long way: from house to house on the Underground Railroad, and all the way to Philadelphia. Here’s today’s question, the one I keep circling in my paper: when Harriet finally gets her freedom, what does it feel like, and is anything missing?

That’s me in the top sentence, and unfeelingly is the author’s word, not mine. I was feeling plenty. Look at how the talking is held in: the marks around it, the comma tucked inside before the said. The bottom one is me too, and it’s lost all of that. Put the marks where my words start and stop, the comma inside the last one, and a capital letter on my name. Then a period.

One of those sentences has me watching from a window, and I’ll not say whether I do. That isn’t what you’re checking. Some sentences are right and some aren’t. Tap only the wrong ones. Find the person doing the thing first. One, or more than one? Then look at the end of the doing word and see if it agrees. Say it aloud if you’re not sure. Wrong ones jar. Leave the right ones be.

The courage box is about the night Anne saved the Barry baby. Matthew told me. I never saw a case of croup in my life, and I’ll say plainly she knew what to do and I wouldn’t have. So that’s one kind of courage, being afraid of a real thing and going anyway. There’s another kind this week. Being afraid of a thing you made up yourself. Watch for which one this chapter is.

I sent her through that spruce grove for a lesson and a warning, and I said I’d risk it, and I did. She came back over the bridge with her teeth chattering. Whether I was right you can decide. I’ve decided already. I usually have. Now say what you noticed, and show it from the chapter. Not from what you’d have done. Nobody asked what you’d have done. They asked what happened.

It’s Marilla. Imagination as a trap, the question says. Well. I could have told you that a year ago, and I believe I did. So watch for the moment a made-up thing stops being fun. Then there’s the last of the week’s word work, and it’s the checking kind, where some of what you see is already right. Don’t go fixing what isn’t broken. I’ve had enough of that from Anne.

Three questions. The first is about the bottle and how it got where it was. The hint points at me, and I won’t argue. The second is about why Anne couldn’t smell it. She told me, through a good deal of crying. Find what she said. The third is about Mrs. Allan coming up the stairs. Look for the small thing she asks to see. It tells you more than a speech would.

One sentence from the start of this chapter, the day the schoolmaster left. I never thought him worth two handkerchiefs, but there it is. Now say it three ways. Change the doing word first. Then start the sentence somewhere else, with a when or a where. Then tell how. Anne could do this in her sleep, and frequently does. You’ll do it awake.

The top sentence is a plain one, and it’s correct. Look at what makes it so. The names start with capitals, the doing word tells you it’s already done, and it stops where it should. The bottom one is about me and my vanilla, and it runs two thoughts together without a breath. Find where one stops and the next starts. Then give my name its capital. I’d thank you to.

Anne baked a cake. Anne bakes a cake. Anne will bake a cake. Same girl, same cake, and I’d wager she does all three before the week is out. What changes is when. Sort the cards by when, then give each group a name of your own. Don’t wait for mine, I haven’t given you any. And say them out loud. Your ear knows more grammar than you think.

Four boxes of word work, and I’ll not pretend they’re exciting. But a girl who can’t tell what’s done from what’s coming is a girl who mixes up her bottles. Two of these are sorting. Put each card where it belongs, then name the groups yourself. Nobody’s going to name them for you. One is typing in a missing piece. Look before you type. I never saw the good of guessing.

There’s a box here about being seen. I’ll be honest, I didn’t hold with that kind of talk once. A child was fed and clothed and that was that. But there’s a new minister’s wife in Avonlea, and Anne has fallen for her entirely. Watch how Mrs. Allan looks at Anne. Not at what Anne does. At Anne. Then watch whether I do the same. I’m not saying I will.

Well. You’ve read it now, so I needn’t tell you what was in that bottle, or whose fault it was. I said partly mine, and I stand by partly. Now you write. Put things in the order they happened. Use the book, not your memory of it. And when you get to Mrs. Allan, use her own words. They’re better than mine, and I’m not too proud to say so.

Two word parts this week, and each one points a direction. One means against, like a thing that pushes back. The other means away, or down, like leaving the house, or going down the cellar stairs. Read the four words in the box, cover the front, and see what’s left. Then ask which way the front is pushing. Against, or away and down. That’s all there is to it.

Two stops, and the first one comes when the cake goes wrong. Read slowly up to the tea. Count who’s at the table, and who’d tell whom. When you reach the stop, think about what Mrs. Allan does, not only what she says. Then read on to the end and listen to what Anne says to me after. I had an answer for her. You can decide whether it was a fair one.

Six words, and every one ended in a y before something got added. Sometimes the y stayed put and sometimes it turned into an i. That isn’t whim. Look at the letter sitting just in front of the y, and then look at what got added after it. Sort them by what happened, then name your three groups. A rule you work out yourself sticks better than one I hand you.

Four words, and one of them I’d never say myself. Vivacious. Anne would, and often. Read the sentence above each card before you flip it, the way the box shows you with the first. The words around it will tell you more than you think. Two of those sentences are about Mrs. Allan, and you’ll meet her today. I think well of her. Guess first, then flip. Not the other way round.

It’s Marilla. The question says watch how one small mistake turns into a big embarrassment. Well, I’ve watched a good many of Anne’s. This one happens in my own kitchen, with the minister at my table, so you can imagine I have opinions. First there are two word parts that point a direction, and some doing words that tell you when. Then the chapter. Mind the bottles.

The box says a place decides how big a mistake feels. I’ll tell you why that’s so in Avonlea. Everybody knows everybody, and nothing stays in a kitchen. Rachel Lynde will have heard before the dishes are dry. So as you read, ask who’s close enough to see, and who’ll hear about it after. Then ask whether the same mistake would matter in a town where nobody knew your name.

Anne’s cake is a story you can only tell in order. The bottle first, then the guests, then the first bite. Tell it backwards and nobody laughs. Today you’re giving the middle of your own story its order. Three scenes, and each one starts with a word that says when. First, then, after that. Pick the ones that fit, not the fanciest. I’d take plain and right over fancy and wrong any day.

The first question asks what color her hair really turned and what had to be done about it. I was the one who had to do it, and I’ll say no more. The second asks how she saved herself, and who came along after. The third gives you her own list and asks you to choose one. Use her words. She chose them carefully enough.

One long sentence with more than one past doing word in it. Tap only the ones that don’t take the usual ending. There’s more than one, so don’t stop at the first. Read it slowly, a word at a time, and ask of each one, did this already happen, and how did it change to show it? I’ve no patience for halfway work. Find all of them.

Four pieces of word work. One is a matching game, and one asks you to remember words without any help. Then two where you tap. Tap only what the directions ask for, not everything that looks interesting. Anne does whatever catches her eye, and I’ve seen where that leads. Read the directions twice. Then do exactly that, and nothing more.

There’s a box here about learning from mistakes. I’ve had a front seat for most of hers. The brooch, the Haunted Wood, the cake with the liniment in it. Every one of them happened on my watch. What I want to know is whether she ever learns anything from them, or only finds a new way to be wrong. Read, and judge for yourself.

Now the writing. I’ll say what I’d say to Anne. Answer the question that’s asked, not the one you wish had been asked. If it wants what happened, say what happened. If it wants a reason, give one, and show where in the book you found it. Plain answers. You can be as romantic as you like in your own story. Not here.

Matching today. Two roots and two little front parts, and what each one means. You met the roots before. The front parts are new company. For each one, think of a whole word you already use that has it inside, and say it out loud. Then take that word apart. What’s left over usually tells you what the part means.

One stop, at the end of the first chapter. Think about what that scrape teaches her, about strangers, and about wanting to look different. Then read on into the second. I was away that afternoon, over at Carmody, so I only learned of it afterward. Watch who comes along, and watch what she says to him. I have my own opinion. Form yours.

I wasn’t there to see this, but I can tell you what happened from the sentence alone. A boy jumps into a boat, and his cheeks are red. Three things, and you know he’s angry and he’s leaving. She doesn’t tell you what he thought. She doesn’t need to. When you write yours, pick three things somebody could see, and trust your reader with the rest.

Six words, and each one once ended in a quiet e. In half of them the e stayed, and in half it was dropped. Tap only the ones where it was dropped. Look at the first letter of what was added. That letter decides whether the e is still needed. It’s a plain rule. I like plain rules. They don’t argue back.

The same four words as yesterday, and no cards this time. Match each one to its meaning. If you’re not sure, put the word in a sentence about somebody at home. I could think of one for every word on that list, and I’d rather not say who. Don’t guess. Guessing is how a girl ends up believing a stranger at the back door.

It’s Marilla. Two chapters, and two scrapes, and I was home for only one of them. The question is what Anne learns from her mistakes, and she will tell you herself, at some length. First there’s word work. Find every doing word in the past that breaks the usual rule, and every word that lost its quiet e. Then read. Then tell each chapter short. Shorter than she would.

The box says the hard part is leaving out the good bits. That child could make a funeral out of a broken teacup, so I know exactly what it means. These two chapters are full of things you’ll want to tell. Most of them you won’t need. Keep why something happened. Let what it looked like go. And if a detail only makes you laugh, it goes first.

Today you cut something. One sentence that wanders off from the scene, even if you’re fond of it. Then move one, to where it does the most good. The last sentence of a scene is the strongest spot. I’ve never seen the use of saying a thing twice, so this suits me. A good story, like a good kitchen, has nothing lying about that doesn’t belong.

The first question is about the doctor’s message. I took it seriously, and I’d do it again. The second wants two changes in her, one you could measure with a tape and one you’d only hear. The third is about me, and that night. Be fair to me. I’ll own I had a cry, and Matthew caught me at it. The book doesn’t say I was wrong.

Here’s one plain sentence about a girl and some books. You’re to say it three ways: add a time, change the doing word, then stretch it out. Anne used to stretch every sentence until it snapped. Miss Stacy taught her better. Try all three, then ask which says the most with the least. That’s the one a sensible person would keep.

The top sentence is Miss Stacy’s opinion, by way of Anne, and I happen to agree with it. Short words are stronger. Find the joining word, and the two that compare. The bottom one is two sentences run together, and somebody’s name has lost its capital. I made those dresses myself, so you’ll forgive me for wanting it written properly.

Some verbs do something. Some only join a person to a description and do no work at all, rather like certain neighbors I could name. A few go either way, depending on the sentence. For those, put each one in two sentences of your own and see whether it’s doing a job or just standing there. The box at the bottom has a test. Use it.

Four pieces of word work, and two of them ask you to sort into three piles, not two. That third pile is where the thinking is. Don’t push a word into a pile because it looks like its neighbor. Say it in a sentence first. I sort the mending the same way: what’s finished, what isn’t, and what I’m not sure of yet.

There’s a box here about noticing your own change. Anne noticed hers, and said so. I noticed it too, standing beside her one day and finding I had to look up. I’ll not say what I did about it that night. Matthew caught me at it, and that’s more than enough witnesses. Read, and watch who sees the change, and who only feels it.

Here’s where you write it down. I’ve no patience for answers that wander. Read the question, decide what it wants, and give it that, with something from the book to show you didn’t make it up. Anne is learning to be her own sharpest critic. Read over what you write once before you call it done. You’ll find something. Everybody does.

Two old roots today, one that means to look and one that means to build. They don’t stand on their own. They sit inside other words the way the yeast sits inside the bread. You never see it, and you’d notice fast if it weren’t there. When a blank stumps you, ask whether the word is about seeing or about making. That will tell you which root belongs there.

Two stops. The first comes when she tells me what she’s been worrying over, on Sunday afternoons of all times. Listen for why growing up feels serious to her, not just that it does. The second comes near the end, and it’s about me. I’d rather you didn’t dwell on it. You will anyway. Keep an eye on how much she talks. Then on how much she doesn’t.

Comparing words. Some take a short ending, some need more or most in front, and some have a y that must change first. Count the beats in the plain word before you decide. Clap them if you must; I won’t tell anyone. Anne used to pile on the longest words she could find. These days she counts more carefully, and so should you.

Four words, and two of them describe Miss Stacy. Mrs. Lynde has her doubts about Miss Stacy, which is reason enough to learn them. Read each sentence before you turn the card. Then, when you match, try each word against a person you know. If it fits nobody at all, you’ve likely got the wrong meaning.

It’s Marilla. That child grew two inches in one summer, and somewhere along the way she stopped chattering. I can’t say I expected to miss it. The question is how a girl can change and stay the same at once. First there are verbs that do nothing at all but join, and words that compare. Then the chapter. Watch what Anne says out loud, and what she only shows.

The box talks about the big idea of a story. Anne says hers right out loud in this chapter, and she says it to me. That’s the easy one. The harder one nobody says. Watch what she chooses, and how it turns out, and what the title is a picture of. A brook doesn’t ask permission to become a river. It simply does.

Editing. This is the part of writing I understand best. It’s like going over a floor with a lamp after you’ve swept it: you find what you missed. Today it’s a capital at the start and a stop at the end of every sentence. Read one line at a time, slowly, with your finger under it. Slow is how you catch things. Fast is how you miss them.

Word work first. It’s ordinary work, and I’ll tell you something about ordinary work. After Matthew, the cows still needed milking and the bread still needed baking, and I found the doing of it held me up. So take this the same way. One blank at a time, one word at a time. Do each one properly, and the next one will come.

There’s a box here about being the one who carries it. Anne carried a great deal those first days. There were neighbors in and out, and there was me, and she kept herself steady for all of us. I didn’t see what it cost her until later. Read, and watch what she does in front of people, and what she saves for when she’s alone.

Now you write. Take your time with these. One asks what happened that morning, one asks why Anne wanted to be alone, and one asks about laughing again. That last one surprised her. She told Mrs. Allan, not me, and I don’t blame her. Answer each one plain and true, with something from the book to show it. Then rest a minute before the workshop. I’d recommend it.

This sentence is about me, and I’ll own it. I heard her, and I crept in. Notice the writer didn’t say I walked, or marched, the way I generally do. Crept is a careful word. It tells you somebody was trying very hard not to make things worse. When you write yours, choose that verb slowly. One right word can say a great deal.

It’s Marilla. Today’s question is about grief, and how it moves. I’ll be plain, the way I always am. Matthew died, and this chapter is about the days after. Anne couldn’t cry at first. Then she could. There’s word work to do first, and that’s no bad thing. It steadies the hands. Then the chapter. Go gently with it.

Somebody is talking in this sentence, and saying two things at once, which is one more than most people need. Each part wants its proper ending. Two words have been squeezed short and need their marks. One little word is standing small when it ought to stand tall. Study the model before you start, and then do it neatly. I’ve no patience for slapdash work.

No word bank today. Every plural has to come out of your own head. These are the words that won’t follow the ordinary rule, and there’s no reasoning with them. One mouse, two mice. One tooth, a whole row of teeth. You simply have to know them, the way I know where every dish in my pantry goes. Say each one aloud before you type it. If the ordinary ending sounds silly, it’s wrong.

Now then, word study. I’ll tell you what I tell Matthew: a job done properly the first time saves doing it twice. Today’s word parts both mean with, or together. That’s how Matthew and I have run Green Gables all these years, the two of us together. Soon there’ll be a boy to lend a hand as well. Work steadily, and check as you go.

Matthew ought to be back from the station by now. I’ve been listening for the buggy. It’ll be a relief to have a sturdy boy about the place, with Matthew getting on in years. You have two chapters today. As you read, don’t just take anybody’s word for how they feel. Watch what they do, and what they say, and what they leave unsaid.
