Well. A girl. I sent word for a boy, plainly and properly, and Mrs. Spencer brought a girl. What use is a girl on a farm? That’s what I said to Matthew, and he said perhaps we could be some use to her. I don’t know what’s come over him. Now it’s your turn. Say what you noticed, and point to the words in the book that show it.

Every word you build today starts with a part that means together. Here’s a sensible way to choose its spelling. Say the word aloud and mind your lips. If they press shut for the next sound, that part ends in an m. If they don’t, it ends in an n. There’s no guessing needed. Your own mouth will tell you, if you’ll only pay attention to it.

Look at the last letter of a word before you do anything to it. That’s plain good sense. If the word ends in a hissing sound, it needs a little extra to make it more than one, or nobody could say it. If it ends in a y with a consonant in front, the y has to change. Most words just take their letter and behave themselves. I wish more people did.

A word is only worth knowing if you can put it to use. Read each sentence right through to the end before you choose. The words around the gap will tell you what belongs there. Placid is a word I approve of. It means calm and steady, which is how a sensible person ought to be. Imagine, I’ve less use for. But you’ll need it this week, so learn it all the same.

Marilla Cuthbert here, and I’ll be guiding your lesson today. Matthew has driven over to Bright River to fetch the boy we sent for, and I’ve everything ready for him. Today’s question is how a writer shows you what somebody feels without saying it outright. By the end, you’ll be able to point to the very words that prove it. We’ll put some awkward plurals in order, too.

A word can carry an opinion the way a basket carries eggs. When somebody calls a thing plain, or useless, that’s a judgment, not a fact. You’ll meet two of us today, Matthew and me, and we don’t always choose the same words about things. As you read, catch one word that sounds like me and one that sounds like Matthew. Then ask who’s doing the judging.

You’re writing about disappointment, and that’s a hard feeling to put on paper. I saw plenty of it in my own kitchen, and not once did that child just tell me she was disappointed. She couldn’t eat. She hid her face in her arms. Let your character do something like that, or say one thing, or go very quiet. Then stop, and let the reader feel the rest.

Now then, word study. Two word parts this week, and both of them tell you where a thing stands. One means under. The other means between. I find myself between two things just now, a mistake I didn’t make and a child I didn’t send for. So I’ll be glad of some plain, orderly work. Take the words one at a time, and check as you go.

White Sands at last. Mrs. Spencer will sort this out, and the child will go where she was meant to go. This week’s word is belonging, and I’ll say this much: a person belongs where there’s a proper use for them. That’s plain sense. As you read, watch the child’s face whenever somebody talks about where she’s to go. Faces tell more than people mean them to.

Well. I went to White Sands to send her back, and I came home with her still beside me. Mrs. Blewett would have taken her, and I’d heard what she’s like to work for. Then I saw the child’s face. I told Matthew she may stay. It seems a sort of duty, and I’ll leave it at that. Now it’s your turn. Say what you saw, and prove it from the book.

Each of these words comes with its own sentence from the book. Read that sentence right through before you so much as touch the card. Then look inside the word for any part you know. Only then turn it over and check. Guess first and check after, and a word stays with you. Flip the cards as fast as you can, and it’s gone again like a hen out of the yard.

Marilla Cuthbert again. I’ve the buggy out and that child beside me, and we’re bound for White Sands to have Mrs. Spencer’s mistake put right. Today’s question, I’m told, is what I might see in her that would change my mind. Well, my mind is made up, and I don’t change it lightly. Read, and judge for yourself. We’ll also sort out the little mark that shows a thing belongs to somebody.

People don’t change all at once. I certainly don’t. If a person changes at all, it starts small: a pause, a second thought, a thing done that doesn’t match what was said. Today you’re to watch me, of all people. Write down what I mean to do at the start. Then mark the very moment I stop and think, and ask yourself what I’d just seen.

You’re building a character today, with one thing she wants and one thing she’s afraid of. Make them real, not just feeling words. That child never told me she was afraid of Mrs. Blewett. She sat perfectly still and stared at her, and her face was pale as anything. That told me plenty. Give your character a want and a fear as plain to see as that.

All four of today’s jobs are tapping jobs, matching or picking out words. If a match won’t go, don’t keep jabbing at it. Stop, read both sides again, and think. That child loses her way the minute her mind wanders, and so will you if you hurry. Go steadily. If one beats you, leave it and come back. The others will make it easier.

I’ve never brought up a child before, so I suppose the two of us are beginners. This week’s watch is about learning what nobody taught you. If you come to a place where she’s plainly out of her depth, stop there a moment. Ask yourself what you’d do in her shoes. Would you own up, or bluff it? Then read on and see which she chooses.

Well. I told the child to say her prayers, and she told me she never said any. Nobody had taught her. So she’s learning the Lord’s Prayer, and she asked if she might call me Aunt Marilla. I said no. Now, before you type a word, go back and find the places in the book you’ll need. Keep a finger on each one while you write.

Marilla Cuthbert again, and I’ll be at your elbow all lesson. Today’s question is what you do when everybody around you knows something you were never taught. That’s a hard spot to be in, so don’t rush it. While you read, keep an eye out for an old habit starting to bend. And in word study, you’ll be hunting for the words whose apostrophe shows they own something.

Here’s how I’d go about it. Before you start the chapter, settle in your head how that child has always done things, in other people’s houses. One plain habit will do. Then, as you read, watch for somebody asking her to do it differently. Does she go along with it? Keep hold of the one thing she won’t give up. You needn’t write it. Just carry it with you.

Here’s how I’d start. Put your character alone somewhere real, a bedroom or the top of the stairs. Then ask what they’d wish for, if nobody could hear. That child made friends out of a reflection and an echo when she was lonely. Your character might do something quite different. Borrow one of the sentence starters if you’re stuck. Write it in their words, not yours.

The first question is about the dresses I made. Look at what she said when she first saw them, and at what she didn’t say. For the second, something happened on the road to church that nobody has told me about yet, so you’ll have to find it yourself. It’s small. Read slowly. The third quotes her exactly. Before you answer, count how many girls in that class had what she didn’t.

Word study, and there’s a new word part this week. It means above, or across, or too much, and I dare say you’ll meet it more often than you’d like. Work through the four boxes in order. In each one, read the whole thing before you start tapping and typing. Most mistakes I’ve seen come from starting before you’ve looked. Check as you go, not at the end.

The child starts Sunday school this week, and she’ll meet other children there, which she’s had little enough of. This week’s watch is friendship. I’ve never had a great deal of use for it myself, but I’ll say this: a friend is somebody you choose, and who chooses you back. As you read, notice whether she has anybody like that yet, and what it costs her that she hasn’t.

Well. She went to Sunday school alone, since I had a headache coming on, and came home and told me it was horrid. Mr. Bell’s prayer was too long, Miss Rogerson asked a great many questions, and every other girl in the class had puffed sleeves. I ought to have scolded her. The trouble is, some of what she said I’ve thought myself for years. Your turn. Say what you noticed, and show me where.

Marilla Cuthbert here, guiding you again. Today’s question is about wanting something and being told no. You’re to watch how the author shows the wanting and the disappointment in the very same breath. Keep hold of one thing you want yourself that somebody has called foolish. It’ll help you understand her. In word study there’s a new word part, the one that means above, or too much.

Here’s how to go about it. Before you open the book, settle what you’re looking for: one thing the child decides to do, even a small one. When you find it, don’t move on. Back up a line or two and find what happened just before. That’s your cause. Then read a little past it and see who has to deal with what she did. Hold all three in your head together.

She gave up the Avery to stay with me. I told her I couldn’t let her sacrifice herself, and she laughed and said there was no sacrifice. That’s Anne for you. Now, don’t just tell me she grew up. Anybody can say that. Put the girl at Bright River beside the girl at the gate and let them speak for themselves. Well. There it is.

The box says courage is doing the hard thing while you’re still afraid. Well now, I’m not a brave man. Going up those stairs to talk Anne into apologizing, when Marilla had told me not to interfere, that was about my limit. But I went. So watch for that. Not somebody who isn’t scared. Somebody who is, and does the thing anyway. And watch what the other people do while she’s doing it.

I went to Carmody for the doctor and there wasn’t one, so I went clear to Spencervale, and it was the small hours when we got back. And it was over. Anne had done it. I walked her home and she talked the whole way, and I let her. Now it’s your turn to say what you noticed, and I dunno that you need to say much. Just say it with the book open.

You met these four yesterday. Well now, I forget words the day after I learn them, so here’s what I do. Say the word, then say the meaning, and listen to whether they sit together. If it sounds like two strangers, it probably is. Do the pair you’re surest of first, and then the next, and the last two nearly match themselves. And if you get one wrong, read the little line that comes up.

Well now, it’s Matthew, and I’m your guide for these two chapters. The question up there says the hard part of Anne’s past turns into a gift. I dunno how yet. I can believe it, though. Anne never had much, and she made the most of every bit. So as you go, keep an eye on who freezes and who moves. Then there’s doing words to find, and some c’s and g’s that don’t behave.

Marilla and I look at Anne and see two different girls. Marilla sees the mistakes. I see, well, I dunno what I see. The girl. And it’s not that one of us is wrong. It’s what each of us has lived through. So do what the box says. One sentence for each person, then ask what they’ve been through that makes them see it that way. That’s the whole gap, most times.

Three questions. The first is about what I noticed about Anne’s dresses. Look at the other girls, then look at Anne. The second is about the store, and why I got so mixed up. Look at who was behind the counter. The third is about the whole week, and who really saw Anne. You get to pick. I’d not pick me, if I were you. But you pick.

Well now, the top sentence is me, and it’s put together proper. A capital on my name, a capital on Anne’s, a capital on Christmas. The bottom one runs two things together, the unwrapping and the watching. One thing finishes and then the next one starts. Put a stop where the first is done. Then capitals on both names. I never was much for writing, but I can see where a thing ends.

These are sentences about Anne’s fall off the Barry roof, and after. Some tell the when right, and some don’t. Look for the word that says when, like yesterday or tomorrow. Then see if the doing word agrees with it. If the two of them argue, tap it. If they get along, leave them be. Marilla and I don’t always agree either, but we generally know when we don’t.

Four things to do, and in two of them some of it’s already right. I’d go careful there. When I went to the store, well, never mind about the store. I got flustered and said yes to things I didn’t want. Don’t you do that. Read each one through. If it’s right, leave it be. Only tap what’s wrong. The other two are matching and choosing. You’ll manage.

There’s a box here about being seen. Well now, I dunno much about that. I’m not one people look at, and I like it that way. But I look. I’ve been looking at Anne for most of a year, and lately something has been bothering me about her that I can’t put my finger on. As you read, look at what I’m looking at. Then you’ll know what I know.

Well now. A rake. And twenty pounds of brown sugar. Marilla’s never going to let me forget the sugar. Now you write about it. I guess you could make me sound foolish, and you’d not be wrong. But look at why I went at all. That’s the part worth writing about. Use the book. It’s got it about right, though I’d have left out the sugar.

Well now, this is the matching again. Two word parts and two roots, and you’ve seen them all week. Tap one, then tap its partner. If you’re not sure, say the whole word out loud, and think about going down the cellar stairs, or going away down the lane. Then ask which way the word points. I’m no scholar. But I know down from away, and so do you.

One stop, at the end. It asks why it was me that noticed. Well now, I’ve wondered that myself. Read the start slow, where I’m sitting in the corner. Then read the store part as fast as you like. It goes about as well as you’d expect. When you get to Christmas, slow down again. That’s the part I’d want you to see.

Six words, and some of them are spelled wrong. Well now, a wrong word looks wrong if you look at it long enough. Say each one slowly and picture where the y went, or where it should have gone. If you’d be embarrassed to see it painted on a store sign, tap it. I’ve seen a few store signs in my time. Leave the good ones alone.

Five ways to show you know your words, and you only pick one. Well now, I’d pick the one about teaching it to somebody younger. I learned more explaining things to Anne than I ever did at school, and I didn’t go long. Pick whichever one you can finish. Then do it all the way through. A thing half done is a thing you’ll be thinking about for days.

Well now, it’s Matthew. The question says I do the bravest thing. I dunno about bravest. It was the hardest, I’ll say that. Today there’s a sentence to fix, and word work where some of it is already right, so you leave that part alone. Then the chapter. You’ll see a dress in it. I’ll not say any more, or I’ll get flustered.

The box says try moving the scene somewhere else. Well now, I’ll help you. Put me in a store where a man’s behind the counter, and I do all right. Put me in a store I don’t usually go to, with somebody I don’t expect behind that counter, and, well. You’ll see. As you read, ask which parts could happen anywhere at all, and which parts only happen here.

Well now, today you just finish it. That’s all. Get to the end. It doesn’t need to be good yet. Anne wanted puffed sleeves for a long while, and it took me till Christmas. A rough ending is better than none. Write two or three sentences, what happened and how your kid feels. Then read the whole thing top to bottom. You might be surprised.

The first question is about how Anne heard her news. The second is about something I said to her, coming back from the pasture. I meant every word of it. The third question is about a line the writer put in, not anybody in the story. I’ll leave that one to you and the book. Read it slow.

The top sentence is Anne’s, in all the fuss. She wanted to write home right away, and I’m mighty glad she did. Find the little helper word and the word it helps. The bottom one runs two sentences together, the way folks talk when they’re in a hurry. Split it, and give the names their capitals. Anne always did care about a name being done right.

One long sentence, and you’re to tap every helper in it. There’s more than one, and some stand right next to each other. Don’t tap the words doing the real work, just the ones helping. It’s a bit like a barn raising. Lots of folks hold the beam, but only one swings the hammer. You want the folks holding the beam.

Four bits of word work. One is matching, one is remembering, and two ask you to tap. Tapping is easy to do too fast. I’ve found most things go better slow. Plowing, for one. Read every word before you tap it, and ask yourself if you’re sure. If you’re not, leave it be a minute and come back. No harm in that.

There’s a box here about knowing a good evening while you’re still in it. Anne’s better at that than I am. She notices the sky and the pointed firs and the old Snow Queen, and she says so out loud. I just walk along beside her. Read slow today, the way she would. Take your time over the happy parts. They’re worth it.

Now the writing part. I’m not much of a talker, so here’s the short of it. Read each question till you know what it wants. Answer it plain, and show where in the book you found it. You don’t need fancy words. Anne’s got enough of those for the both of us. Just true ones.

Two old roots again, the writing one and the throwing one, and two little pieces that go on the front. Match each piece to what it means. If you get stuck, think of a word you know and say it slow. I’m no scholar. But Anne says the old roots are like seeds. You plant one, and a whole row of words comes up.

There’s one stop, near the end, when Anne and I are bringing the cows in. She says something about the boy we sent for, and I say something back. You’ll get to it. Before then, there’s the morning the news comes out, and the commencement. I was there for that. I didn’t say a word till she’d finished reading her essay.

Here’s a little paragraph somebody wrote too fast, and three words in it got their endings put on wrong. Tap only those. The rest are fine, and tapping a fine one won’t help you any. Say each word slow in your head, and look at the spot where the ending joins on. That’s where the trouble usually hides. Same as with fences.

Same four words as yesterday, and now you match them up without the sentences to lean on. That’s how you find out what stuck. If one won’t come, try to remember the sentence it lived in. Anne says words have a home sentence. I wouldn’t know about that. I just know one of these words sounds an awful lot like her, once she’s set her mind.

Well now, it’s Matthew. Today’s question is about two feelings sitting side by side, glad and worried, in the very same day. I dunno much about books, but I know that feeling. First there’s word work, roots and helping words. Then you read about the day the results came out, and Anne coming home. Watch for the happy parts. And notice where folks are fretting, too.

The box says you can tell how a person’s grown by what they wish for. When Anne first came, she wished she could stay. That was about all she wanted. I remember it pretty well, being the one driving the buggy. Today, listen for what she wishes for next. Then set the two wishes side by side. That’s quite a road to come down, I reckon.

Today you score your own story, row by row, then fix just one thing. Just one. I like that. When a fence needs mending, you don’t tear the whole fence down. You find the one rail that’s loose, and you put it right. Be honest with your scores. Nobody’s going to think less of you for a two.

Marilla’s the one for rules, but I’ll do my best. The sentence you’re fixing is somebody talking, and excited about it. There’s a little word at the front that wants a pause after it. There’s a word squeezed short that’s lost its mark. And the talking itself wants something around it, both ends. Look at the one that’s done right first. It shows you every piece.

Some words don’t do what you’d expect. You’d think one child, two childs. But no. They change on the inside instead. We had a bit of that at Green Gables this week, if I’m honest. Somebody arrived who wasn’t what we’d planned for. Look through the sentence and find every word that won’t follow the ordinary rule. There’s more than one.

Well now, words. I’m a farmer, not a scholar, but I know a good tool when I see one, and these word parts are tools. Two of them mean with, or together. I’ve been thinking about that word, together, more than usual lately. You’ll see why when you read. For now, work through these the way you’d work a field. One row at a time.

I’ll not tell you what happened at the station. That’s yours to read. But I’ll say this much. I drove eight miles there expecting one thing, and eight miles home with something quite different beside me. Listen to what she does with every plain thing we passed, the road, the pond, the trees. I’ve never looked at that road the same way since.

Here’s something I didn’t know till lately. That word, companion. It comes from an old word for bread. A companion was somebody you shared your bread with. I like that. Sitting beside someone on a long drive is a bit like sharing bread, I suppose. Match up the parts, and notice how each one carries its own little piece of the meaning.

Take your time with this chapter. It’s a long drive, and most of it is talk. As you go, keep a count of how many things get given a brand new name. I lost count myself, somewhere past the pond. And when you reach the end, sit still a moment before you go on. Ask yourself what somebody who names everything might be hoping for.

Marilla’s a great one for doing things properly, and she’d want these spelled right. Here’s how I’d go about it. Say the word as more than one, and listen. If your mouth needs an extra bit at the end, or a y at the end has to change its ways, that’s one to tap. The plain ones just add their letter and carry on.

Four words today, and you met every one of them yesterday. Placid. That was me, mostly, before this week. Imagine. That was never me, not much. Companion, and delight. Well, I’ll let you work out who those belong to. Match each one to its meaning. If one gives you trouble, don’t fret. Say it out loud, slowly, and it often comes back.

Hello, it’s Matthew Cuthbert. Today I’ll be guiding you through your lesson. I’m not much of a talker, so I’ll keep it short. Today’s question is about voice, what makes a person sound like themselves and nobody else. I met someone once who sounded like nobody I’d ever heard. By the end of this lesson, you’ll be able to say what made her voice her own.

Now, here’s a thing I’ve noticed. When a story gets told about me, the teller knows things I never said out loud. That’s the narrator. Then there’s what I’m thinking, sitting on that buggy seat. That’s me. Keep the two apart today. When a plain old road starts sounding beautiful, ask yourself who’s doing the seeing. The narrator, or somebody else?

Now it’s your turn to make somebody talk. Anne didn’t just see a road. She gave it a name nobody else would have thought of. That’s her voice, in a handful of words. Before you write, decide on one thing your character would call by a name of their own. Then let them say it out loud. Don’t tell us about them. Let them talk.

For the first question, think about what I’m like with people, and what it cost me to climb those stairs. That’s your clue. For the second, find the part where Anne says sorry and read it again. Notice how she says it, not just what. For the last one, look back over what you wrote earlier this week. You may already have the moment written down.

Four jobs today, and one of them you get to choose. Take them one box at a time. If one goes wrong, it’s no great trouble. You can always try again. I never got anything right the first time myself, not even driving the mare. After the words there are two drafts to fix, like a careful editor. Read those slowly, out loud if you can.

Anne hasn’t come down, and Marilla won’t say why. I’ve been hanging about the kitchen like a lost calf. This week’s watch is belonging. If you want a way to keep track of it, notice every time somebody does a small kind thing without being asked. I’d keep a count. Belonging doesn’t come with a speech. It comes in little things like that.

Well, now you know. I went upstairs. I hadn’t been up there in four years, not since I helped Marilla paper the spare bedroom. I asked Anne if she’d just smooth it over, and she said she’d do anything for me. Don’t tell Marilla I had a hand in it. Now, go and find your answers in the book. Take your time. I’ll wait.

There’s one stop, at the very end, so you can read straight through. Some of this chapter is funny, and you’re allowed to laugh. When you reach the end, though, stop before you turn to the questions. Read the stopping question and sit with it for a bit. Think about what one small thing might mean to somebody who’s never had it.

Hello, it’s Matthew Cuthbert again. I’ll be with you today. Here’s the question. By the end of this chapter somebody calls Green Gables home, and you’re to work out what had to happen first. It’s the last day of the week, so you’ll look back at how far somebody’s come. And you’ll play editor, finding apostrophes that went astray. Take it slow. That’s how I do things.

Before you read, take a moment and picture Anne at White Sands, sitting quiet while grown-ups decided where she’d go. Hold that picture. Then as you read today, watch for one small thing she does that the girl at White Sands couldn’t have done. When you find it, you’ve measured how far she’s come. And watch whoever’s standing next to her. They may have moved too.

Well now. I drove to Bright River for a boy, and there she was, sitting on a pile of shingles with a carpetbag. She talked the whole way home. I didn’t mind. I liked it. When you pick your picture, look at what she noticed that day. A girl who calls a plain old road the White Way of Delight… well now. That tells you something about her.

These three questions build on each other. The first asks when and who. The second asks what was happening. The third asks who stood against it. Put them together, and you have the whole shape of the war in a few sentences. That shape is what you’ll carry into the novel.

Here is one plain sentence about the end of the war. Your job is to say it three different ways: a new beginning, a stronger verb, and a detail about where or how. Writers have practiced this way for hundreds of years. Each new way shows you something the first sentence left out.

The top sentence is a model, and every capital in it is there for a reason. Look at the names of places, months, and people. The bottom one has lost all of its capitals, and it’s really two sentences squeezed into one. Find where one thought ends and the next one begins.

Some words stand in for people: she, they, him, them. They don’t all do the same job. Some do the action, some receive it, and a couple can do both. Sort them by the job they’re doing, then name the groups yourself. Names you give stick better than names you’re given.

Four kinds of word work today. Some of it asks you to notice before anyone tells you the rule, and that’s on purpose. A rule you find yourself stays with you longer than one you’re handed. So go slowly at the start, look hard, and make your best guess before you check.

This quarter we watch for courage, and here is the first thing to know about it. Courage isn’t the same as not being scared. It’s being scared and doing the right thing anyway. Even reading about a hard time in history takes a little of that. If today’s facts feel heavy, that’s all right. Stay with them. That’s the first small brave thing.

Now it’s your turn to write. The questions ask you to go back to the passage, so keep it open beside you. Use the passage’s own facts, the dates and the names, to show how you know. Then you’ll finish with a short piece of your own writing.

This week we’re building a bridge, one word at a time. Two small word parts at the front of words will do the building. One means across, and one means forward. Read each meaning first, then choose the part that fits. Every right choice lays a plank. By the end of the week, the bridge will reach the other shore.

The passage is short, and it covers six long years. Watch for two things: the countries that were taken over, one after another, and the countries that joined together to stop it. When you reach the pause questions, stop and think about a child your age living in one of those places.

Long words from history often hide two vowels working together to make one sound. The trick is that the same pair doesn’t always sound the same. Say each word out loud, slowly, and listen for what the pair is really saying before you sort it. Your ear knows more than you think.

These four words will follow you all through the new book. Each one is about what can happen to a country, and to the people in it, during a war. Read the sentence, take the word apart, then make your guess before you flip the card. Guessing first is how a word starts to belong to you.

Welcome. You’ve just said goodbye to Anne and Green Gables, and a new book is close. Before we open it, we spend this week on the true history behind it. Today’s question is how World War Two began, and who started it. First you’ll warm up and do some word work. Then a short reading, and a few questions to answer in your own words.

Today’s reading move is a bit like packing for a trip. A novel set in real history expects you to bring some facts along. As you read, collect the names of countries, leaders, and dates, like things going into a suitcase. When the story starts next week, you’ll be glad they’re already packed.
Transport. To carry across.
Translate. To carry meaning across languages.
Progress. To step forward.
Protect. To cover in front; to shield.

Your writing project this quarter is an opinion essay, and it starts with one simple skill. A fact can be checked. An opinion is what someone thinks, and someone else could disagree. Today you’ll practice telling them apart, using things from your own life. Soon you’ll use the same skill on the new book.

Two of today’s questions are about differences: how Denmark was treated compared to other countries. A difference needs two sides, so name both. The last question asks about the Resistance. Think about why someone would choose to join, knowing it could be dangerous.

Today you get to choose which sentence to fix. Both have the same kind of trouble: missing capitals, and two thoughts run together. Pick one, then look back at the model at the top. Notice which words there are names. Names of people, countries, and groups always start tall.

In each sentence, more than one of these stand-in words is hiding. Your job is to find only the ones receiving the action, the ones the action happens to. A quick test helps: try swapping in he, or him. If him sounds right, you’ve found one.

Today’s word work asks you to find things, not just sort them. In grammar and spelling, you’ll hunt through a passage and tap only what fits. That’s harder than it sounds, because the right answers are hiding among ones that look almost right. Slow down, and check each one before you tap.

Today’s Courage Watch is about Denmark’s king, Christian the Tenth. He didn’t fight with weapons. Instead, during the occupation, he kept riding his horse through the streets of Copenhagen, often with no guards around him. People saw him, and knew their king hadn’t given up. Sometimes courage is simply showing up, again and again, where everyone can see you.

Time to write about what you read. Keep the passage close, because each question points back to a part of it. You’ll also study one sentence closely and then try its shape yourself. Then you’ll finish with today’s step in your own writing project.

The bridge’s first span is already built. Today you lay the next four planks. The same two word parts are at work: one means across, and one means forward. Some of these words may be new to you, so let the meaning lead you, not the sound of the word.

This passage is about how things looked on the surface in Denmark, and what was really going on underneath. Watch for the reason the German leaders had for keeping things calm. Then watch for the people who quietly pushed back. Stop at each pause question before you move on.

Today’s sentence is built in two halves. The first half tells you what someone wanted. Then two small words, so that, turn the corner and give you the reason. Writers use this shape when the why matters as much as the what. When you write your own, make the second half do real work.

Most vowel pairs say what you expect. Today you’re hunting for the ones that don’t. Say each word slowly, and listen. When a pair sits in a part of the word you say quickly, it often goes soft and mumbly. Those are the ones that trip up even grown-up spellers.

Today’s words come straight from the reading about Denmark, so you’ll meet them again in just a few minutes. Read the sentence above each one, and look for clues around it. One of these words is about giving up. Another is about the people who run a country. See if you can tell which, before you flip.

Welcome back. Today we zoom in on one country, the one our new book is set in: Denmark. Germany took it over in a single day. So what was everyday life like after that? You’ll warm up, work with some words, then read about Denmark under the Germans, and study one sentence the way a writer would.

Today’s reading move is about numbers. A date or a time in a history passage can say more than it seems to. When you see a number, stop and ask what it meant for the people living through it. A few hours. One morning in April. Turn each number into a picture of real people.
Transparent. Clear enough to see through.
Propel. To push forward.
Transplant. To move a plant to new ground.
Produce. To make, or bring forth.

Last time, you learned that an opinion is something people could disagree with. Today that opinion becomes a claim: one clear sentence that takes a side. No maybe, no kind of. Practice on something you care about, like the best pet or the best season. A clear claim makes everything after it easier.

The last question is the most interesting one today. A story can be untrue and still tell you something true about the people who told it. Ask yourself what the Danes wanted to believe about their king, and about themselves. Then use the passage to show how you know.

Pick the sentence you’d like to fix. Both have the same troubles: lost capitals, and two sentences pressed together. Look closely at the model on top. Some words there are names of peoples and groups, and those always take a capital, wherever they fall in the sentence.

This time you supply the word yourself. Read each sentence and ask one question: is the missing person doing the action, or is the action happening to them? That decides which form you need. Use the word bank, and say each finished sentence out loud to check it.

Today the word work asks you to build, not just find. You’ll choose the right word and write it in yourself. When you’re unsure, say the sentence out loud with each choice. Your ear often catches what your eye misses. Then check, and fix anything that didn’t sound right.

Today’s Courage Watch is about ordinary people: teachers, fishermen, doctors, neighbors. Most of their courage was small and quiet. A doctor who wrote a different name on a hospital record. A neighbor who kept a child safe for a week. One small act doesn’t look like much. Thousands of them, together, saved thousands of lives.

Time to write. Today’s questions ask you to explain a law, compare Denmark to other countries, and think about a story that isn’t exactly true. Take your time with that last one. You’ll also try the writer’s sentence shape from the reading, and take today’s step in your own writing.

Two spans of the bridge are finished, and the lamps at their ends are lit. Today you build the third. The same two word parts are doing the work, one meaning across and one meaning forward. Read every meaning all the way through before you choose. The meaning is your map.

This passage begins with what happened in many countries, and then it turns. Watch for the word different. That’s where Denmark’s part begins. There’s also a famous story in here that isn’t quite true. As you read, think about why people might keep telling it anyway.

Look at where today’s sentence pauses. The writer could have stopped early. Instead, a dash holds you still for a moment, and then two more words tell the harder truth. A pause like that makes the end land with weight. Writers save it for the words that matter most.

Today you fill in the missing vowel pair yourself. There are two decisions for each word: which pair belongs, and how it sounds in that spot. If you’re stuck, say the whole word slowly and stretch out the middle. The sound usually points to the pair.

Today’s words come from the reading about the yellow star. Some of them are hard words for a hard subject, and they matter. Read the sentence above each one carefully. Think about what the word is doing in that sentence before you guess. Then flip the card, and see how close you came.

Welcome back. Today’s reading is about a law the Nazis made in many countries, forcing Jewish people to wear a yellow star. It’s a hard subject, and an important one. You’ll also learn how Denmark’s answer was different. Then you’ll study one sentence that says a hard truth very carefully, and try writing one like it.

Today’s reading move is holding on to a puzzle. Sometimes a fact doesn’t make sense yet, and that’s fine. Mark it, make a guess, and keep reading. The new book is called Number the Stars. Keep that title in your mind today, and see whether anything you read helps it make sense.
Transfer. To carry from one place to another.
Provide. To make something available.
Transform. To change form.
Promote. To move forward, like moving up to a higher rank.

A claim has to be something a person could argue with. If no one could ever disagree, it’s just a fact. Today you’ll test your claims. Could a smart, fair person say no? If not, change it until they could. That’s when a claim is ready for reasons.

The last question asks what made Denmark’s rescue so unusual. To answer it well, you need to compare. Think about what happened to Jewish people in other countries, and then what happened in Denmark. Name a specific fact from each side. A comparison is only as strong as its facts.

Choose your sentence. Both are run together, with capitals missing. Today the model is about fishermen and the sea. Look at which words in it are names of peoples and countries. Then make your sentence into two clean sentences, each with a capital at the front and an end mark at the back.

This is a draft with a few mistakes in it. Some sentences use the wrong form of a stand-in word, and some are already right. Read each one out loud. When something sounds off, try swapping in he, or him, to check. Tap only the sentences that need fixing.

Today’s word work is review, with a twist. Some of what you see is already correct, and some isn’t. Your job is to tap only the mistakes. That means reading every item carefully, even the ones that look fine at first glance. Careful readers check before they change.

Today’s Courage Watch is about remembering. Almost everyone in Denmark’s rescue story is gone now: the fishermen, the families, the king. One kind of courage is choosing not to forget them, and not to forget the people who were hurt. The author of our new book wrote it so that we would remember. Reading it is how you join in.

Time for the week’s last writing. The first two questions are about the rescue itself. The third asks you to look back across all four readings, so think about the whole week, not just today. Then take your last step in this week’s writing project.

Three spans are finished, and their lamps are lit. Today you lay the last four planks. When the final one is down, the bridge reaches the far shore, the shore of our new book. Read each meaning, choose the part that fits, and watch the bridge reach across.

Today’s passage has a warning, a time of hiding, and a journey across the sea. Watch for all the different kinds of people who helped. Not one hero, but many. When you reach the pause questions, think about what each person risked. And watch for the German man who sent the warning.

These words come from a draft, and some are misspelled. The mistakes are mostly in the middle of the word, where the vowels go soft and quiet. Say each word slowly, then picture how it really looks. Tap only the ones that are wrong, and leave the correct ones alone.

Today’s words come from the story of the rescue. Each one names a part of what happened: a warning, a plan, a secret journey. Read the sentence above each word, and picture the moment it describes. Then guess, and flip to check. You’ll meet ideas like these again in the novel.

Welcome back. This is the last history day before we open the novel. Today’s reading tells about October 1943, when the Nazis planned to arrest all the Jewish people in Denmark, and what ordinary Danes did about it. It’s a story about fear, and about courage. When you finish today, you’ll be ready for the book.

Today’s reading move is putting things side by side. Today’s passage is the fourth one this week, and each one explains a little of the next. As you read, look back at the other three. Ask how the occupation, the star law, and the king help explain what happened in October 1943.
Transaction. A trade, or an exchange, between people.
Prolong. To make something last longer.
Transcript. A written copy of what someone said.
Pronounce. To say a word out loud.

Next week, you’ll write claims about Number the Stars. Today you practice choosing. Write a claim on two different topics, then ask which one you could give the most reasons for. The best claim isn’t always the one you feel most strongly about. It’s the one you have the most to say about.

When I was a girl, we had a shelf of books in our front room, the same as every family. My father kept one book on that shelf that I was never allowed to touch. I didn’t ask why. You learned not to ask. Look at this one, from the museum in Copenhagen. From the outside, it’s only a book. That was the whole idea.

Two of today’s questions ask you to find something small: one detail that shows life isn’t normal, and the careful way Annemarie answers. The last question is about her mother’s worry. Think about why being noticed by a soldier could be so dangerous.

Here is one plain sentence about the race in Chapter 1. Your job is to say it three new ways: a new beginning, a stronger verb, and a detail about where or how. Writers have practiced like this for hundreds of years. Each new version shows you something the first one couldn’t.

The model sentence is about two girls on a street. The sentence to fix has lost its capitals, and two thoughts are squeezed together with no stop between them. One name in it also needs a tiny mark to show that something belongs to someone. Use the model to help you.

Some words show who owns something without using any apostrophe at all. Others look almost the same but mean something different. Sort these into three groups, then name the groups yourself. The little apostrophe will turn out to be the biggest clue.

Today’s word work starts with noticing. In grammar and spelling, you’ll sort before anyone tells you the rule. That’s on purpose. Look hard, make your best guess, and then check. A rule you find yourself stays with you much longer than one you’re handed.

Today’s Courage Watch is about a very small kind of brave. When I was a girl in Copenhagen, we learned not to stare at the soldiers, and not to give them a reason to notice us. Annemarie is ten, and she is frightened. But she answers carefully and stays calm. Sometimes courage is simply choosing your words when your heart is pounding.

Now you’ll write about what you read. Keep the chapter close, because each question points back to a detail in it. Then you’ll start the next part of your opinion writing. This time it’s about the book, and about a moment of courage you choose yourself.

This week we light a night sky, one star at a time. Two old roots do the work. One means to break. The other means to lead. Read each meaning, then choose the root that finishes the word. By the end of the week, the whole sky will be shining.

As you read, keep an eye on the corner of the street. Notice what the soldiers are wearing and carrying, and how each girl acts when they’re stopped. Little Kirsti doesn’t act the way the older girls do. Ask yourself why. Stop at each pause question before you go on.

Say each of these history words out loud, slowly. Somewhere in the middle, a vowel goes soft and quiet, and you can’t tell which letter is spelling it. Sort them by the letter that’s hiding there. Then try saying a related word, where that part gets loud again.

These four words will follow you all week. Each one has a job in this story: stopping something, behaving a certain way, being moved, and the feeling that something is wrong. Read the sentence, take the word apart, and guess before you flip the card.

Hello again. It’s Grete. Last week I told you the history. This week I’ll tell it the way a storyteller does. I’m made up, the same way Annemarie is made up. But the Copenhagen I’ll describe is real. Today, the book begins. Three girls race down a street, and two soldiers stop them. Today’s question: how does the author show that danger hides in ordinary things?

This week’s reading move is about small things. In this book, danger rarely shouts. It stands on a corner, or asks one quiet question. When a small detail feels odd, stop and finish this sentence in your head: people only act this way when… Today, listen closely to how Annemarie answers.
Interrupt. To break in between, the way a shout breaks into a race.
Erupt. To break out, the way a volcano does.
Conduct. To lead together. It also means how a person behaves.
Introduce. To lead someone in, and help two people meet.

Your writing this week is about the book. Today you only have to choose a moment from Chapter 1 where someone shows courage or loyalty. Be specific. Not just that she’s brave, but exactly what she does. A specific moment gives you something real to argue about in the next lesson.

Look at the people on bicycles in this photograph. My grandmother could have been one of them. She told me she would ride out early, just to be on the street when the king came by on his horse. She said he would lift his hand, and for one minute the whole street felt like Denmark again. No guards. Just a king, and his people.

For the second question, the answer the boy gives is short, but it carries a lot. Explain what it means, not just what it says. For the third, two feelings sit side by side in Annemarie. Name both, and find the detail that shows each one.

The model is a short sentence about a king and his horse. The sentence to fix is longer. It joins two complete thoughts with the word and, and it needs a small mark before that word. It also needs a capital on the name for the people of Denmark.

Every sentence here has more than one owner-word hiding in it, and a couple of look-alikes with apostrophes. Tap only the words that show who owns something. If a word can be read as two words, like it is, leave it alone.

Today’s word work asks you to hunt. In grammar and spelling, more than one answer is hiding in each set, and some of the words that look right are not. Read every word before you tap. Slow and careful wins here.

Today’s Courage Watch is about remembering. King Christian rode his horse through Copenhagen almost every morning, often with no guards at all. My grandmother used to stand on the pavement just to see him pass. Watching him was a way of saying: we still remember who we are. Sometimes courage is simply refusing to forget.

Now you write. Two questions are about the king and the famous answer the boy gave. The third is about Lise, and that one needs care. Then you’ll turn the moment you chose last time into a claim: one strong sentence that takes a side.

Last time you lit the bowl of the Big Dipper. Today, four new words light its handle. The roots haven’t changed: one means to break, and one means to lead. Watch the meanings closely. They’ll tell you which root belongs.

This chapter has a story inside a story. Watch for the moment Annemarie stops telling a made-up fairy tale and starts remembering something true. Notice a famous answer a boy once gave to a German soldier. And notice the sister Annemarie hardly ever talks about.

Today’s sentence holds one moment open. A question has been asked, and instead of giving the answer, the writer shows a girl shaking her head, waiting. That little pause makes you need the next line. When you try it, freeze your character just before the answer arrives.
Most of these words hide a soft, quiet vowel. Today you’re looking for the ones that don’t. Say each word out loud. If every part comes out clear and strong, that’s one to tap.
Today you match this week’s four words to their meanings. Before you tap, try saying each word in a sentence about Annemarie. If you can use it, you know it. If you can’t yet, the match will help.

Hello, it’s Grete. Today Kirsti wants a fairy tale with a king in it. But Denmark had a real king, and I remember him well. You’ll warm up, work with some words, read Chapter 2, then study one short sentence the way a writer would. Today’s question: what does King Christian the Tenth mean to the Danes?

Today’s reading move is about the gap between then and now. When a character remembers something ordinary from before the war, ask: could that still happen today, on these streets? The space between the memory and the present is where you’ll find the danger.
Corrupt. To break down what is good, and make it dishonest.
Bankrupt. A broken bank. Out of money.
Deduct. To lead away, to take an amount off.
Product. Something led forward into being. Something made.

Last time you chose a moment. Today it becomes a claim. A strong claim has three parts: who, which virtue, and exactly how they show it. Look at how Sam sharpens his. Then build yours, one part at a time, and put it together into one clear sentence.

Our kitchen looked a lot like this one. In the evenings we did our homework by candlelight, because the electricity was rationed, and my mother cooked on a little burner like the one on that table. The best place in the whole flat was next to it, where it was warm. And the radio, oh, we kept the radio turned down very low.

For the last question, think about Peter’s visit as a clue. It isn’t only who he is. It’s when he comes, and how the grown-ups behave once he’s there. A visit at that hour, in a city with rules about being out at night, tells you something.

The model sentence names a person and a place, and every capital in it is there for a reason. The sentence to fix is really two sentences run together. Find where the first thought ends. One name also needs a mark to show that something belongs to someone.

Each sentence is missing one owner-word. The word bank has four choices, and none of them needs an apostrophe. If you feel like adding one, stop. Ask yourself: does it mean it is, or they are? If not, leave the apostrophe out.

Today you build. In grammar and spelling, you’ll type the right word or letter yourself instead of choosing it. There’s a word bank to help. Watch out for the apostrophe trap in grammar, and in spelling, say a related word to hear the hidden letter.

Today’s Courage Watch is about noticing. A locked shop is easy to walk past without a word. Annemarie doesn’t walk past. She asks her parents what it means. In my Copenhagen, many grown-ups looked away, because looking away felt safer. Paying attention, and asking the hard question, is its own kind of brave.

Time to write. The first question asks you to describe the shop door, so use details from the chapter. The second asks why the Germans closed certain shops. The third asks about Peter’s visit. Then you’ll give your claim three strong reasons.

The Big Dipper is finished. Today we cross the sky to a smaller group of stars. The two roots are the same: one breaks, one leads. Two of today’s words begin with a part that means away or off, so read every meaning all the way to the end.

Watch the shop door closely: what is on it, and what language is the sign written in? Then, at home, notice who comes to visit, and what time it is when he arrives. Notice how the grown-ups talk to each other in front of the girls. Stop at each pause question.

Today’s sentence names a feeling but hides the reason. The writer uses one vague word, something, and that makes you lean in and guess. That’s how suspense works. When you write your own, tell your reader how it felt, but keep the why a secret.

Each word is missing the quiet letter in the middle. Don’t guess by sound, because the sound won’t tell you. Say the related word next to it, the one where that part is loud and clear. Then type the letter you hear.
Match the four words again. This time, before you tap a meaning, say it out loud in your own words. If you can explain a word to someone else, it belongs to you now.

Hello, it’s Grete. Today a broken button sends the girls to a little shop they’ve known all their lives. What they find there changes how Annemarie sees her street. You’ll warm up, work with words, read Chapter 3, and study one sentence closely. Today’s question: what does a closed shop tell us about what is happening in Copenhagen?

Today’s reading move is about objects. A lock or a sign is a small thing on the page, but someone with power put it there. So when you see one, ask two questions. Who did this? And who is it aimed at? The answer to the second one is where the danger is.
Abrupt. Broken off suddenly.
Disrupt. To break apart, and throw everything into confusion.
Produce. To lead forward, to make.
Reduce. To lead back, to make smaller.

Your claim says what you think. Today you add three reasons that say why. Look at how Sam turns one big reason into three specific ones, each about something different Annemarie does. Make each of your reasons a clear sentence of its own.

I didn’t go to the synagogue. My family went to church on Sundays. But my friend Ruth did, and I remember the morning before the New Year, when she came to our door with her mother, both of them very quiet. They didn’t stay long. Years later I understood: they were passing on the warning, door to door, the way the rabbi had asked.

For the second question, look for the word the grown-ups use for what the Nazis plan to do. Then explain what Annemarie understands it really means. The difference between the polite word and the truth is the whole point.

The sentence to fix is about real history, and it’s full of names that need capitals: the name of a group, the name of a people, and the name of a country. Look back at the model to see how a sentence begins and ends.

This little draft about Chapter 4 has some apostrophes that don’t belong. Owner-words like hers, its and theirs never take one. But a name, like Lise’s or her sister’s, does. Tap only the sentences with a real problem.
Today is review, and some answers are already correct. In grammar and spelling, tap only the mistakes. If you tap one that is fine, it costs you. So read each one twice before you decide.

Today’s Courage Watch is about being trusted. Annemarie’s parents decide she is old enough to hear the truth, and that means she is old enough to be brave with it. When I was ten, my father told me something I had to keep to myself. I remember feeling frightened, and proud at the same time.

Now you write. The questions ask what Annemarie learns tonight, what one careful word really means, and how her life is different by the end of the chapter. Then you’ll find proof in the book for each of the reasons you wrote last time.

This is the last night of stars. Four words climb the handle of the Little Dipper, and the last one leads you to the North Star. The two roots you know are here again, plus one new word about water. Read the meaning, find the root.

The first part of this chapter is light, almost funny. Enjoy it, and ask yourself why the author put it here. Then notice the room getting quiet once Kirsti is asleep. Listen to how carefully the grown-ups choose their words, and notice what changes for Ellen tonight.

Georg Duckwitz was a German. He worked for the very government that planned the raid. When he learned the date, he could have stayed silent. Instead he secretly told Danish leaders, and the warning spread. Years later, Israel honored him as one of the Righteous Among the Nations, a title for people who risked themselves to save Jews.

This is Rabbi Marcus Melchior. On the morning before the Jewish New Year in 1943, he stood in front of a full synagogue and told everyone the Nazis were coming in two days. Don’t stay at home, he said. Tell everyone you know. Because people listened, and passed it on, most Danish Jews were warned in time.

Some of these words are spelled correctly, and some have lost their hidden letter. For each one, say the related word, the one where the quiet part gets loud. If the letters don’t match what you hear, tap it.
Last match of the week. See if you can do it with no misses at all. Then try one more thing: say all four words in one sentence about Chapter 4. It’s harder than it sounds.

Hello, it’s Grete. Today’s chapter starts with paper dolls and a little girl who hates her new shoes. It ends with a secret told after dark. You’ll warm up, work with words, read Chapter 4, and collect two new cards about real people. Today’s question: why was this the moment Annemarie’s parents had to tell her the truth?

All week you’ve been noticing small signs: soldiers on a corner, a king who rode alone, a lock on a shop door. Today, add up the clues. One small sign might be nothing. Four signs pointing the same way are a pattern. Ask what all of them, together, are telling you.
Aqueduct. A stone channel that leads water to a town.
Deduce. To lead your thinking to an answer, like a detective.
Induce. To lead someone into doing something.
Disrupt. To break apart. Last word, and the North Star shines.

Your reasons say why you believe your claim. Today, you prove them. For each reason, find one moment in Chapters 1 to 4, and write where it happens. A strong piece of evidence is specific: something a character does or says that anyone could find in the book.

In Copenhagen, nobody ever made my friend Ruth wear a yellow star. Denmark refused. I didn’t see one of these stars until after the war, in a museum. I stood in front of it for a long time, thinking of Ruth, and of how different her life could have been if Denmark had said yes. Ellen’s star is different. Nobody made her wear it. It’s hers.

These questions ask you to look closely at small things: a chain, a photograph, a mark on a hand. Ask yourself why the author chose such tiny details for such a frightening night. Sometimes the smallest thing on the page is carrying the biggest feeling.

Here is one plain sentence about the necklace. Your job is to say it three new ways: a new beginning, a stronger verb, and a detail about where or how. The bones of the sentence stay the same. But each version makes a reader feel the moment a little differently.

The model is short and plain. The sentence to fix has someone asking a question out loud, so it needs quotation marks and a question mark in the right places. Two sentences are squeezed together, too, and one describing word needs a small joining mark.

Every action needs someone to do it. Read the sentence and find each little word that stands in for a person, then look at the verb right beside it. Some verbs have an extra ending and some don’t. What decides it? That’s the rule you’re here to find.

This week’s word work starts with noticing again. Nobody tells you the rule first. In grammar, you’ll look at who is doing each action. In spelling, you’ll look for words that have been built from smaller parts. Find the pattern yourself, and it will stay with you.

Today’s Courage Watch is about courage that has only seconds. When I was a girl, I saw a woman on a tram drop a paper she shouldn’t have had. Her friend stepped on it before anyone noticed, without a word. I’ve never forgotten how fast she moved. Watch Annemarie in this chapter. She doesn’t stop to think. She acts.

Now you write. Each question points at a small moment: what Annemarie does with her hands, what Papa does with the photographs, and what she finds in her palm afterward. Then, in your essay, you’ll learn to set a short quote inside your own sentence, so it fits smoothly.

This week we leave the city for the sea. Two old roots do the work. One means to believe. The other means to stretch. Each stretching word reaches a beam of light across the water, and each believing word lights a window on the far shore. Read the meaning, then pick the root.

This chapter is short, and most of it happens in the dark. Read slowly. Listen for sounds: boots, voices, doors. Notice what Annemarie sees that the soldiers must not see, and what Papa reaches for when the questions get dangerous. Stop at each pause question before you go on.

Lots of long words are really short words wearing extra pieces: something added at the front, something added at the end, or both. Tap each word that’s been built this way. Then ask yourself: if I took the pieces off, what word would be left underneath?

Four new words follow you through Chapters 5 to 8. One is about planning, one about being believed, one about keeping quiet, and one about how your body feels when you’re afraid. Read each sentence, take the word apart if you can, and make a guess before you flip the card.

Hello, it’s Grete. In this chapter, it’s the middle of the night, and someone is pounding on the Johansens’ door. Annemarie will have only seconds to decide what to do. You’ll warm up, work with words, read Chapter 5, and try saying one sentence three ways. Today’s question: what does courage look like when there’s no time to think?

This week’s reading move is about proof. It isn’t enough to say a character is brave. You have to point to the exact moment, the thing she does, and say what could have gone wrong. As you read, keep one finger ready. When Annemarie acts, mark the spot.
Credible. Able to be believed.
Credit. Trust that someone will pay you back.
Intend. To stretch your mind toward a plan.
Extend. To stretch out, farther and farther, across the water.

Your essay starts to sound like real writing now. A quote dropped in by itself feels bumpy, like a stone in your shoe. Today you learn to give it a set-up before it and a so-what after it, so the reader knows exactly why it matters.

We had a telephone just like this one, black and heavy, on a small table in our hall. My mother told me never to say anything important on it. Once I heard her tell my aunt that the apples were ripe, in the middle of winter. Later I asked her about it. She only smiled and said that some apples ripen early.

The middle question asks why Papa speaks almost in code. To answer it, think about who else might hear a telephone call in 1943. Then think about Ellen. What does it cost a ten-year-old to say goodbye without knowing when she’ll see her parents again?

The model is about a trip. The sentence to fix is really two sentences run together. Find where one complete thought ends and the next one begins. Then check the name at the very start, because names always stand up tall.

Some of these sentences have a name doing the action, and some have a pronoun. Only the pronouns and their verbs count today. That’s the tricky part. Before you tap, ask yourself: is this a little stand-in word, or is it a person’s name?

Today the word work asks you to hunt for two things at once. In grammar, you’ll find both the person-word and the action that goes with it. In spelling, you’ll catch pieces added at the front and pieces added at the end. Keep both in your head as you go.

Today’s Courage Watch is about the grown-ups. Mama doesn’t make a speech. She just packs, smiles, and gets three girls on a train. My own mother was like that. When she was most worried, she talked about the weather and buttered our bread. It took me years to understand that her calm was her courage.

Now it’s your turn to write. The questions ask about the family’s plan, why Papa talks the way he does, and what Ellen has to leave behind. Then you’ll write the opening of your essay: a hook that drops the reader into a moment, and your claim.

Two more reaches of light across the water. The roots are the same, believing and stretching, but the words are new. One of them is about papers that prove who you are. That mattered a great deal in 1943. Read each meaning carefully before you choose.

Listen closely to Papa on the telephone. Every word he says sounds ordinary. Ask what it might really mean, and notice how Annemarie starts to wonder too. Then you’ll ride the train north along the sea. Keep an eye on the door at the end of the train car.

Read this sentence again, slowly. The writer doesn’t stop to print the whole phone call. She keeps her own sentence moving and tucks Papa’s words inside it. That’s a trick you can borrow for your essay, when you want to share what someone said without dropping in a big, clunky quote.

This sentence is a short trip on the train. Hunt for words with an extra piece on the front, and words with an extra piece on the end. One word even has two pieces on the end. Careful: a word that only looks built doesn’t count.

In the last lesson you met these four words with a sentence and a flip card. Now see if they stuck. Match each word to its meaning. If you miss one, don’t worry. Read the meaning again, and say it to yourself in your own words.

Hello, it’s Grete. After the soldiers leave, nobody in the Johansen family sleeps. By the end of this chapter, they’re on a train going north, and Papa has made a very strange phone call. You’ll warm up, work with words, read Chapter 6, and study one sentence the way a writer would. Today’s question: why do people speak carefully when danger is near?

Today’s reading move is about choosing small. When you prove a point, you don’t need the whole scene. You need the few exact words that do the job. As you read, listen for a short phrase a grown-up says, one you could copy word for word to show courage.
Credentials. Papers that make people believe you are who you say you are.
Discredit. To make people stop believing someone.
Contend. To stretch yourself against something; to struggle.
Tendon. A tough cord that stretches from a muscle to a bone. The light reaches farther.

An introduction does two jobs. First it pulls the reader in with a real moment from the book. Then it says plainly what you believe. Keep it short. A confident first paragraph of three sentences beats a long one that wanders.

My grandmother lived up near the coast, north of the city. From her garden you could see Sweden on a clear day, a gray line across the water. When I was little, it was only a view. But in the autumn of 1943, I noticed the grown-ups looking at that gray line differently. It took me a long time to understand why.

The last question asks why Sweden is important. You don’t need to know anything that hasn’t happened yet. Look at what the girls can see from the shore, and remember what you learned about Sweden earlier in this unit. Then explain what a free country so close by might mean.

The model is one calm sentence about a house. The sentence to fix has two sentences joined with no stop between them, and some names that need capitals: two girls and one country. Use the model to help you.

Getting the verb to match its person-word isn’t about being fussy. When they don’t match, a reader trips. Read each sentence in a whisper and trust your ear. Then fix the last sentence, which has two mistakes, and say which word made you choose each fix.

Now the word work asks you to use what you’ve figured out. Study each model first. In grammar, you’ll pick the verb that matches its person-word. In spelling, you’ll join parts into one word, and some letters will try to trick you. Go slowly on the last line.

Today’s Courage Watch is about keeping something safe for someone else. When I was young, a neighbor gave me a small box to keep, and asked me to tell no one. I never opened it, and I never told. It felt like the most grown-up thing I had ever done. Watch what Annemarie promises Ellen in this chapter.

Time to write. The questions ask about the necklace, what it means to Ellen, and why Sweden matters so much. Then you’ll write the first body paragraph of your essay. It has a reason, a piece of evidence from the book, and a sentence that ties them back to your claim.

Halfway across the water already. Two believing words, two stretching words. One of the stretching words is about acting as if something is true when it isn’t, which comes in handy in this story. Read each meaning, then choose the root that finishes the word.

Enjoy the beginning of this chapter. It’s the most peaceful place in the whole book so far: a meadow, a kitten, the sea. Then notice Mama’s questions when the girls come back from the shore. And pay attention at bedtime, when Ellen asks about something she’s missing.

This sentence does three jobs at once. First you hear exactly what Annemarie says. Then you learn who said it. Then you learn when. Notice how that little tail at the end keeps the words tied to the story. In your own writing, a quote needs a tail like that too.

Adding parts to a word is like hooking cars onto a train. Each new car has to hook on properly. Sometimes a letter doubles, and sometimes a tricky spelling in the middle stays exactly as it was. Join each word carefully, then fix the line that went off the tracks.

Match the words again. This time, try saying each meaning out loud in your own words before you tap. If you can explain a word to someone else, it belongs to you. Listen for these words as you read, too. Sometimes a writer never uses the word, but you can feel it on the page.

Hello, it’s Grete. The city is behind you now. In this chapter you’ll smell the sea, walk through a meadow, and stand at the edge of the water looking at another country. But even here, there’s a secret to keep. You’ll warm up, work with words, read Chapter 7, and study one sentence closely. Today’s question: why can a small object carry so much weight?

Today’s reading move is about sorting. As you read, keep two lists in your head: what Annemarie feels, and what she does. The feelings tell you she’s human. The doing is your evidence. Watch especially for a quiet promise, and whether she keeps it.
Incredible. So amazing it is hard to believe.
Credence. The belief that something is true.
Pretend. To act as if something is true when it isn’t.
Attend. To stretch your mind toward something; to pay attention. The light is nearly there.

A body paragraph works like a sandwich with a purpose. Your reason goes on top. Your evidence from the book goes in the middle. And the last sentence connects it all back to what you believe. You only need one strong paragraph, so choose your best reason.

I saw a boat like this one years later, in a museum. It’s so small. I stood beside it and tried to picture a dozen people inside, lying still in the dark, listening to the engine and the waves. Some of them were children. I think about the fishermen, too, who did this night after night, and went back to fishing in the morning.

For the second question, think back to the phone call in Chapter 6. Where else have you heard grown-ups talk about fishing weather? You don’t have to be sure what it means. A good guess, backed up by what you noticed, is exactly what a careful reader does.

The model is a short sentence about Uncle Henrik. The sentence to fix is about a name nobody recognizes. That name has a title in front of it, and the title needs capitals and a small joining mark. And again, two sentences need to be split apart.

Here’s a little draft with some mistakes and some sentences that are fine. Read each one quietly to yourself. Your ear usually knows before your brain can name the rule. Tap only the sentences that sound wrong, then fix one of them.

This is review, so some of what you see is already right. In grammar and spelling, only tap what needs fixing. Read every line twice before you decide. A good editor knows when to change something, and also when to leave it alone.

Today’s Courage Watch is about keeping quiet. Annemarie can tell something about this family story doesn’t add up. She doesn’t argue. She watches. When I was a girl, I learned that sometimes the bravest person in the room is a child who notices everything and says nothing until it’s safe.

Now you write. The questions ask why the news of a death seems strange, what an odd phrase about fishing might mean, and what Annemarie begins to suspect. Then you’ll draft a second body paragraph, with a new reason and a new piece of evidence.

This is the last stretch of water. Four more words, and the beam can finally reach the far shore. One of these words describes someone who believes things too easily. As you read, ask whether anyone in this chapter is hoping someone will believe a story.

Uncle Henrik is a fisherman, and he talks a lot about the weather. Listen to the phrases he uses. Have you heard one of them before? Then pay close attention near the end of the chapter, when Annemarie hears a name she doesn’t know. Notice what she thinks, and what she says out loud.

This card belongs to Dr. Karl Henry Køster, a surgeon at Bispebjerg Hospital in Copenhagen. In October 1943, he and the nurses and doctors there hid Jewish families among their patients, and in the hospital chapel. One day, a long funeral line of taxis drove away from that chapel. The people inside weren’t going to a funeral. They were families on their way to the boats.

Six built words, and only some are misspelled. For each one, take it apart: the base, the piece at the front, the piece at the end. Then check each part on its own. Usually only one part has gone wrong.

Last match of the week. See if you can do it with no misses at all. Then try something harder: use two of the words together in one sentence about Annemarie at the house by the sea. Discreet and tense might make a good pair.

Hello, it’s Grete. Uncle Henrik comes home from the sea, and something isn’t quite right. A relative nobody has ever mentioned has died, and there will be a casket in the living room. You’ll warm up, work with words, read Chapter 8, and draft more of your essay. Today’s question: what is really going on at Uncle Henrik’s house?

Today’s reading move asks you to weigh courage. When several people are brave in the same chapter, ask what each one could lose. A grown-up and a child might both be brave, but the cost isn’t always the same. Look for the details that show you what’s at stake.
Credulous. Too quick to believe things.
Creditor. Someone who trusts you to pay them back.
Tendency. A leaning toward something, like a habit.
Superintendent. The person who watches over a school or a building. And the light reaches all the way across.

Two reasons are stronger than one. This paragraph has the same shape as the last one: reason, evidence, link. But it needs a brand-new reason and a brand-new quote. If your two paragraphs sound the same, look for a different moment in the book.

After the war, I saw young men in Copenhagen wearing armbands like this one. Before that, nobody wore anything. The resistance was secret. My uncle helped them, I think, but he never said so, and I never asked. He used to say the less you knew, the less anyone could take from you.

Uncle Henrik’s idea about bravery is one of the biggest in the whole book. You don’t have to agree with him. But before you decide, think back to the day the soldier stopped Annemarie on the street. Did knowing less help her then? That moment can be your proof.

Here is one plain sentence about Uncle Henrik in the barn. Say it three new ways: a new beginning, a stronger action word, and a detail about where or how. The bones of the sentence stay the same. But each version puts the reader in a slightly different spot in that barn.

The model is short and plain, a sentence about Uncle Henrik. The sentence to fix has two whole thoughts joined by a small linking word, so it needs a mark that gives the reader a breath. Look for two words squeezed into one, too, and two names standing too small.

Read these sentences slowly and find every word that has been pressed together. Each one hides a missing letter or two. Ask yourself where the little mark sits, and why it sits there and nowhere else. That’s the rule you’re here to find.

This week’s word work is about pieces that go missing. In grammar, you’ll find words that have been squeezed together, with a little mark where letters used to be. In spelling, you’ll listen to the very last beat of longer words. Nobody gives you the rule first. Find the pattern yourself.

Today’s Courage Watch is about asking the hard question. When I was a girl, I knew my father was hiding something in our cellar. It took me three days to ask him. My voice shook. But asking felt braver than pretending I hadn’t noticed. Watch Annemarie in the barn. She asks, and she doesn’t look away.

Now you write. The questions ask how you can tell Annemarie is sure, what Uncle Henrik means about being brave, and why he decides to tell her only part of the truth. Then, in your essay, you’ll stretch one short explanation into two or three sentences.

On this night, there are no lights at Uncle Henrik’s farm. Not one. So the path to the sea has to be found in the dark. This week’s three roots all mean to go, and each right word shows you the next stretch of path. The hard part is the spelling. Listen carefully to each ending.

This chapter starts quietly, in a barn at sunset, with a cow being milked. Don’t let the quiet fool you. Listen to how Annemarie speaks to her uncle, and to the question he asks her back. Then notice what arrives at the farm after dark, and who comes to sit beside it.

Say each long word out loud and clap it. Listen to the last clap. Some words end with a consonant and then a soft L sound, and that ending never comes apart. Tap every word that ends that way, then work out where each word splits.

Four words follow you through Chapters 9 to 12. Two of them are about going and giving way, one is about getting in, and one is about a thing that stands for something bigger. Read each sentence, take the word apart if you can, and make a guess before you flip the card.

Hello, this is Grete. Annemarie has worked something out: the grown-ups are not telling her the truth. In this chapter she goes looking for Uncle Henrik and asks him straight out.
