You’ll warm up, work with words, read Chapter 9, and try saying one sentence three ways. Today’s question: what does Uncle Henrik tell her about courage, and why does it matter?

This week’s reading move is about noticing what keeps coming back. When a book says something twice, or three times, it wants you to stop and look. Keep a short list as you read. If Uncle Henrik returns to the same idea more than once, put a tally beside it.
Proceed. To move forward.
Exceed. To go beyond what was expected.
Concede. To give in.
Access. A way to get in, or to reach something.

One sentence of explanation is often not enough. Today you stretch it. First, say what most people would do. Then show what the character did instead. Then end with a picture the reader will remember. Three small moves, and your reason suddenly sounds true.

The stars come back in this chapter, and they carry a lot. Annemarie thinks about how many there are, and how big the sky is. Ask yourself what else is too many to count, or too big to hold. A symbol can hold more than one idea, so don’t stop at your first one.

The model is about someone reading aloud. The sentence to fix is long, and a lot is squeezed into it: two pairs of words pressed into one, and one name that owns something. Find each spot where letters are missing, and the spot where something belongs to someone.

Read the whole paragraph before you tap anything. Every little raised mark is doing a job, but not every one is doing the same job. Some stand in for missing letters, and some don’t. Slow down at each one, and ask what it’s doing there.

Today you hunt for two things at once. In grammar, a little raised mark can mean letters are missing, or it can mean something belongs to someone. They look the same and do different jobs. In spelling, you’ll catch more than one kind of ending that always stays together.

Today’s Courage Watch is about a calm voice in a dangerous room. Once, a policeman stopped my mother on a bridge and asked where she was going. She smiled and talked about the price of fish. My knees were shaking. Hers weren’t. Watch Mama when the officer stands beside the casket. Listen to how she speaks.

Now you write. The questions ask what Mama does when the soldiers come, what the stars might stand for, and what the casket might really be hiding. Then you’ll zoom in on one single word from a quote, and explain why that word, and no other, is the right one.

The path goes on, a little farther from the farmhouse. Same three roots, all meaning to go, but four new words. One is a short break from your work. One is about getting the result you hoped for. Watch the spelling closely: two of these roots sound almost alike.
This is Psalm one hundred forty-seven, verse four, in the old words of the King James Bible. He telleth the number of the stars; he calleth them all by their names.

Read this chapter slowly. It happens in one room, by candlelight. Notice who speaks and who stays silent, and how each person sits when the boots come in. Then, near the end, someone opens an old book and reads aloud. Listen to those words. Some of them are the title of this book.

Read this sentence aloud, slowly, and notice where your voice pauses. A writer can slip a few words into the middle of a sentence and change where we stand: outside with the sky, or inside someone’s head. Read it once with those words and once without. Feel the difference.

Some endings are so tightly glued that they always travel together: the soft L ending, and the endings that sound like shun and cher. Clap each long word, listen for the last beat, and tap every word that ends with one of those glued pieces.

Here’s the match. Try it without the cards first. If a word gives you trouble, take it apart: does it have one of this week’s go-roots inside it? And for symbol, think of a real thing in this chapter that might stand for something larger than itself.

Hello, this is Grete. Night has come at Uncle Henrik’s house, and the living room is full of quiet mourners and candlelight. Then a car pulls up outside. You’ll warm up, work with words, read Chapter 10, and study one sentence the way a writer does. Today’s question: what do the stars in this chapter stand for?

Some things in a book show up once. Others keep coming back. As you read, keep a little tally for anything you see more than once: an object, a word, a light. The longest tally usually points to the biggest idea. And each time it comes back, ask whether it means something new.
Success. Getting the result you hoped for.
Recess. A short break from your work.
Precede. To go before something else.
Excess. More than you need.

A quote can’t argue for you. You have to do it. Today, pick one single word from your quote and hold it up to the light. Why that word and not another? Say what it isn’t, then say what it is. That’s how a small word starts to carry a big reason.

Every Friday evening, the family upstairs lit two candles in silver candlesticks a lot like these. I could see the glow under their door when I passed on the stairs. When they had to leave, the candlesticks stayed behind on the table. Years later, they told me those were the first thing they thought about in Sweden. Not their beds. The candlesticks.

Be careful with the third question. Peter does say goodbye. But Annemarie answers him with a question, and his answer is only half an answer. Think about what nobody could promise anybody in October 1943. That’s where your thinking should start.

The model is about Peter, and a promise he can’t quite make. The sentence to fix is really two sentences run together, and each one has two words pressed into one. Find where the first thought ends. Then give the second thought a capital to stand on.

Here you get to choose. Pressing two words together changes how a sentence sounds, like the difference between a person talking and a sign on a wall. Fill in each blank. Then, in the last line, listen for whose voice you hear: a person, or a notice pinned to a door.

Today the word work moves from noticing to using. You’ve found the patterns. Now you put them to work: choosing when to press two words together, and splitting long words in the right place. A writer chooses on purpose. That’s what you’re practicing here.

Today’s Courage Watch is about letting go. When the Jewish family upstairs from us left in October 1943, they left the dishes on the table. Mrs. Levin pressed a little brass key into my mother’s hand and said, keep it for us. Watch the Rosens in this chapter. Notice what they had to leave behind, and what they carry with them anyway.

Now you write. The questions ask about the packet Peter hands over, what the candlesticks stood for, and what Annemarie asks Peter when he says goodbye. Then, in your essay, you’ll tie each body paragraph back to your big idea with one strong closing sentence.

Halfway through the woods now. The path is darker here, under the trees. Four more words with the go-roots. One of them is the opposite of coming closer, like the tide pulling back from the beach. As you work, listen to each ending before you choose.

Read slowly when the casket is opened. Watch what Peter takes out, and what he gives to each person. Notice the tiny passenger who needs something to keep her warm. And notice a small packet that changes hands without anyone explaining it. Ask yourself why nobody asks.

Read this sentence aloud and feel where it slows down. Right in the middle, a little mark tells you a list is coming. Then three places, one after another, like steps. Ask why Lowry stops at three. Would two be enough? Would four be too many?

Clap each word before you type anything, and count the claps. Then check your split against your claps. If your split makes a beat you didn’t clap, something’s wrong. Your ears are the best spelling check you have.

Match these four again, and this time, say each word out loud in a sentence about Chapter 11 before you tap. If you can use a word, you own it. If you can only recognize it, it still belongs to the book.

Hello, this is Grete. The casket is open, and the night is not over yet. Peter has things to hand out, and a long, dark walk lies ahead for the Rosens. You’ll warm up, work with words, read Chapter 11, and study one sentence the way a writer does. Today’s question: what does it cost to do the brave thing, even when it works?

Today’s reading move asks you to be a little choosy. Not everything is a symbol, and a reader who calls everything a symbol isn’t really reading. Ask one question about each object you notice: does anyone in the story care about it? If nobody does, it’s probably there to help you see the room.
Succeed. To do well, to do what you set out to do.
Recede. To go back, the way the tide does.
Process. Steps that go forward, one after another.
Secede. To break away from a group.

Each body paragraph needs a knot at the end, or the thread slips out. Today you add one closing sentence to each paragraph, using a key word from your claim. It’s a small sentence, but it reminds your reader why the whole paragraph matters.

My grandmother had a tall clock like this in her hall. It struck every half hour, and at night you could hear it all through the house. On the worst nights of the war, I lay awake and counted the strikes. Every one meant someone still wasn’t home. Annemarie hears a clock like that in this chapter.

The third question asks you to look back across the whole week. In Chapter 9, Uncle Henrik said not knowing can help you be brave. Now Annemarie doesn’t know where her mother is. Does not knowing still feel like a help? Your answer can change. That’s exactly the point.

The model is a short sentence about not knowing where someone is. The sentence to fix is two sentences pushed together. Give the first one an ending, and the second one a capital to start. And look for one pair of words pressed into one, still waiting for its little mark.

This is a full editing pass. Some of these sentences are fine. Some have a little raised mark where it doesn’t belong, or no mark where one should be. Read each sentence slowly, the long way and the short way, and trust your ear.

This is review, so some of what you see is already right. In grammar and spelling, only tap what needs an editor. Read each line twice before you decide. Some of the hardest mistakes are the ones that look almost right.

Today’s Courage Watch is about waiting. During the war, my mother once sat up all night, waiting for my father to come home from a meeting he wouldn’t tell us about. She mended the same sock over and over. Waiting is a kind of courage nobody sees. Watch Annemarie alone in the rocking chair, and notice how she tries to stay calm.

Now you write. The questions ask what wakes Annemarie, why Mama’s absence frightens her, and how her feelings about not knowing have changed since Chapter 9. Then you’ll build one full body paragraph, using every move from this week.

Out of the woods now, and across the meadow. This is the last stretch of path. Four more go-words, and one of them describes a long line of people walking slowly together. When the last word is in place, look down at the harbor. Someone is waiting there.

This chapter is short, so read it slowly. Notice the clock in the hall, and the times Annemarie keeps track of. Notice the light outside the window. Then read the last page twice. After all that waiting, it moves very fast.

This card belongs to two fishermen, Børge Laursen and Jacob Andersen. In October 1943, they took their little boat, Marie, across the water to Sweden about ten times, each time with Jewish families hidden on board. Then they came back, and did it again. Uncle Henrik is made up. These two men are real.

Six words split into beats, and only some are split correctly. Clap each one out loud. If a split gives you a beat you didn’t clap, it needs fixing. Tap only those. Then fix one, and explain what went wrong.

Last match of the week. Try it with no misses at all. Then try something harder: use symbol and one other word together in a sentence about something in Chapters 9 to 12 that stands for more than itself.

Hello, this is Grete. The Rosens have gone into the dark with Mama, and Annemarie is alone in the rocking chair, waiting. This chapter is short and very quiet. You’ll warm up, work with words, read Chapter 12, and finish one full paragraph of your essay. Today’s question: what does it feel like to wait, not knowing?

Today’s reading move is about saying maybe. When you think something is a symbol, point to the exact words first. Then say what it might stand for, and why. A careful reader doesn’t say, this means. A careful reader says, this might mean, because. And then tries a second idea.
Procession. A line of people moving forward together.
Intercede. To step in between, to help someone.
Concession. Something you give up to someone else.
Succeed. To do what you set out to do. And the path reaches the harbor.

Today all the moves come together: a reason, a quote, a zoom on one word, a stretched so-what, and a knot back to your claim. Don’t try to make it perfect. Make it complete. This is the paragraph you’ll polish and publish next.

My mother read us that story from a book with a red cover, and I knew every word. Years later, walking home alone after dark, I said it to myself under my breath, all the way to our door. A story you know by heart is good company when you are frightened. Annemarie seems to think so too.

The third question is the week’s big one. Lowry gives us one girl on one path. The real rescue had hundreds of people, on many paths and many boats. Find one way this scene is like what really happened, and one way it’s different. Both answers can be true at once.

Here is one plain sentence: Annemarie ran toward the path. Say it three new ways. Give it a new beginning, swap in a stronger running word, and add a detail about how she ran. The sentence keeps its bones. But each version shows a slightly different girl running into the woods.

The model is a short sentence about running through the woods. The sentence to fix has three words in it that sound almost alike. Decide whether each one is the right twin for its spot. Then find the place where one thought ends and the next one begins, and give each thought a capital.

Read this sentence out loud and listen. Several words in it have a twin, a word that sounds exactly the same but is spelled differently and means something else. Tap every one. Then try to say the rule. If your ear can’t tell the twins apart, what can?

This week’s word work is about words that sound exactly alike. Say them out loud and you can’t tell them apart. Only the spelling shows which one the writer meant. Nobody gives you the rule first. Hunt for the twins, and work out for yourself how a reader is supposed to know.

Today’s Courage Watch is about being the one who is there. When I was ten, our neighbor fell on the stairs, and her baby was crying alone upstairs. No grown-up was home. I wasn’t brave, only nearest, so I went up. Annemarie isn’t the oldest or the strongest. She is the one who can go. Watch what she decides.

Now you write. The questions ask what Mama tells Annemarie to do, and why, and then for one small detail that shows Annemarie is scared and keeps going anyway. The last one asks you to hold this scene up against the real history from Week 15. Then you write your essay’s conclusion.

Have you ever seen a whole street of windows light up, one candle at a time? This week’s three roots are about shape and about bending, and every right word lights a candle in a window. Some words take the shape root, and some take a bending root. Before you choose, think about what the word is doing.

Chapter 13 starts at dawn, with Mama on the ground at the edge of the meadow. Watch what Annemarie finds near the steps, and who decides what to do about it. Then, on the path in Chapter 14, listen to the story Annemarie tells herself as she runs. Why that story, on this path?

Same hunt, different sentence. Your ear won’t help you here, so slow down and look. Which words have a sound-alike twin? Tap them. Then think about how you’ll remember which spelling goes with which meaning. Some people make up a little trick for each pair.

Four words for the last week of the book. Two of them are about fitting a shape and bending back. Two are about the careful work you’ll do with the Afterword: putting two things side by side, and deciding at the end. Read each sentence, take the word apart, and make a guess before you flip.

Hello, this is Grete. Mama has come home hurt, and something important was left behind by the steps. This is the last week of the novel, and the last week of your essay. You’ll warm up, work with words, read Chapters 13 and 14, and write your conclusion. Today’s question: what does brave running look like when you don’t know exactly why you’re running?

This week, read like a detective with two boxes. One box holds what could really have happened in Denmark in 1943. The other holds what the author shaped to make a good story. Make your two columns. When you aren’t sure where something goes, write the question down. The Afterword, at the end of the week, will help you check.
Conform. To fit in, to match a shape.
Reform. To shape again.
Reflect. To bend back, like light, or a thought.
Flexible. Able to bend. Four windows are lit.

Today you write the ending of your essay. A good conclusion doesn’t just say, the end. It says your claim again in fresh words, names how your character changed, and then looks forward, out of the book and into the real world. Three moves. Sam shows you how first. Then you try.

There was a dog on our street during the war, a shaggy farm dog who barked at everyone. The soldiers’ dogs were different. They were quiet, and they watched. I remember one standing beside a truck, ears up, nose working. I didn’t know then what those noses could find. Annemarie is about to meet two of them.

The second question is about a mystery Lowry chooses not to explain yet. Don’t guess too hard at the answer. Think instead about why an author would hold something back. What does not knowing do to you as a reader, right here, on this page?

The model is a plain sentence about a soldier’s question. The sentence to fix has three sound-alike words, and every one of them is the wrong twin. One should be a number, one should show belonging, and one should mean very. Then find where the first thought ends, and give the sentence a stop.

Every sound-alike word in this paragraph might be right, or it might be the wrong twin. Tap only the wrong ones. Read each one and ask what it has to mean in that spot. A place? Belonging? A number, or very? The meaning decides, not the sound.

Last time you found sound-alike words. This time, some of them are wrong. In grammar and spelling, you’re hunting for the twin that slipped into the wrong sentence. Read slowly. A wrong twin sounds perfect when you say it, and that is exactly why it’s so easy to miss.

Today’s Courage Watch is about courage that looks silly. Once, when soldiers stopped my father’s cart, my mother chattered about the weather and laughed too loudly. I was embarrassed. Later I understood: she was keeping their eyes on her, not on the sacks behind us. Watch Annemarie. Sometimes the bravest thing is to seem like nothing at all.

Now you write. The questions ask what Annemarie does when the dogs sniff the basket, what the chapter keeps secret about the handkerchief, and how this scene compares with the real rescue. Then you revise your essay by reading it out loud and fixing whatever makes your tongue trip.

More windows are waiting on the street. Today’s words all take one of the three roots again. One of them is a word for something your body does before you can even think about it. Ask what each word is about, a shape or bending, and then light the window.

Read this chapter slowly. It’s short, and almost all of it happens in one place, on the path, with the soldiers in front of her. Notice what Annemarie says, and what she lets them see. Notice the dogs, too: where they look, and what they want. And at the very end, watch which way the soldiers go.

This sentence sends the soldiers away, back down the path toward where Annemarie came from. It adds nothing new, and that’s the point. It closes the scene by circling back to where it began. When you write your own, end a moment by pointing it home, back toward the start.

This is the same kind of hunt. Some of these words are the wrong twin, and your ear will tell you everything is fine. Don’t trust it. Look at each word. Then pick one you tapped, spell it the right way, and say what the wrong word really means.

Quick match today. You met these four words in the last lesson, so try to match them without looking back. Then see if you can find a moment in Chapter 15 where Annemarie has to conform, to fit the shape of what the soldiers expect to see.

Hello, this is Grete. Annemarie is alone on the path with the basket, and she hears something ahead of her. This is the chapter the whole book has been building toward. You’ll warm up, work with words, read Chapter 15, and study one sentence the way a writer does. Today’s question: when the soldiers stop her, what does she do?

Today’s reading move: hold one detail up to a fact. Pick one thing from this chapter, like the dogs, or soldiers stopping a child, and turn it into a question a history book could answer. Write the question down. You’re not trying to catch Lowry out. You’re finding where the history ends and the storytelling begins.
Perform. To carry out, all the way through.
Inform. To give someone knowledge.
Reflex. A quick move your body makes without thinking.
Deform. To spoil the shape of something. Eight windows are lit.

Revision is for the ear. Read your whole essay out loud, slowly, the way you’d read it to someone else. If your tongue trips, the sentence is too long. If you hear one word three times, swap one out. If a sentence sounds flat, find a stronger verb. Spelling can wait for the next lesson.

On the day Denmark was free, my father took me into the city. Every shop seemed to be shut. On one door, someone had hung a sign: Closed because of joy. My father read it out loud and laughed until he cried. I have never forgotten that sign. Look at the two young men beside it. Even that day, they kept watch.

The last question asks for your conclusion about Annemarie. Think about the whole book, not just these chapters. Where did her courage start? How did it grow? And remember that real Danes did these things too. A strong conclusion looks back, and then it looks forward.

The model is a short sentence about Uncle Henrik explaining. The sentence to fix uses the same sound-alike word three times, and only one of them is right. One should point to a place, and one should show belonging. Read each in its spot and decide. Then add the marks that separate a list of three.

First you watch an editor at work. Read the before sentence out loud. It sounds perfect, and it’s full of mistakes. That’s what makes these words so tricky. Then fill in each blank by asking what the word means there, and fix one last sentence on your own.

Today you stop hunting and start using. In grammar and spelling, you’ll study how a sentence gets fixed, and then choose the right sound-alike word yourself. Read each sentence for its meaning first. Ask what the word has to do in that spot, and the spelling will follow.

Today’s Courage Watch is about a whole town being brave together. After the war, I learned how many people on our street had helped: the baker, the woman upstairs, the boy who delivered the papers. None of them ever told anyone. Annemarie’s run was one run among hundreds. Listen to how Uncle Henrik talks about the others.

Now you write. The questions ask what the handkerchief did, what Annemarie kept safe all this long time, and what your conclusion is about her courage. Then you’ll run an editing pass on your essay: sound-alike words, contractions, verbs that agree, and capital letters.

The street is getting brighter. Today two words take the shape root and two take a bending root. One of them is a word for clothes that make everyone match. Think about what is being shaped, or what is bending, and light four more windows.

These are the last two chapters, so read them slowly. In Chapter 16, Uncle Henrik answers the questions Annemarie has been carrying, and his answer about the handkerchief is real history. Then Chapter 17 jumps ahead in time. Let it surprise you. Notice what is joyful and what is hard, and how Lowry lets both be true.

This is the very last sentence of the book. Look how small it is. Lowry doesn’t explain the war or tell you what Annemarie learned. She ends on one promise, and she puts the promise last, after the speaker. When you mimic it, end on a short promise, and let it have the final words.

Same move, new sentences. Every answer comes from the word bank, and each one sounds just like two others. So say the meaning to yourself first: belonging, a place, they are, toward, very, or a number. Then pick the spelling that carries that meaning.

Match these four words again, and this time try to do it in your head before you tap. Then look ahead. Two of these words, compare and conclude, are exactly what you’ll be doing with the Afterword in the next lesson.

Hello, this is Grete. Two questions have waited a long time: what was in the handkerchief, and what happened to the Rosens? In these last two chapters, Uncle Henrik finally explains, and the story reaches its end. You’ll warm up, work with words, read Chapters 16 and 17, and edit your essay. Today’s question: what can a novel tell you that a history book never could?

Today, read with two pencils in your mind. One marks the facts, the things a history book could tell you. The other marks the inside of the moment: what Annemarie notices, fears and hopes. At the end, say in one sentence what the story gave you that a list of facts couldn’t.
Transform. To change from one shape into another.
Uniform. One shape, so everyone matches.
Inflect. To bend your voice, to change how a word sounds.
Deflect. To bend something away. Twelve windows are lit.

Last time you fixed how your essay sounds. Now you fix how it looks. Reading aloud won’t catch the wrong sound-alike word, so you have to look at each one. Check your contractions, check that each verb matches its subject, and check every capital letter. That’s editing.

When I was small, my grandfather took me to see the king ride by. He came down the street on his horse with no guards at all, and people on bicycles rode along beside him. My grandfather lifted his hat. I asked why the king wasn’t afraid of the soldiers. My grandfather said, because we are all his guards.

The third question puts your essay next to the real history. Read your claim again, then read what Lowry says about the Danish people. Does your claim still hold? Where does it grow? You don’t have to throw your claim away. You make it deeper.

The model is a short sentence about the author. The sentence to fix has three sound-alike words, and each one is the wrong twin. One should introduce something, one should be a number, and one should mean it is. It also needs a mark that tells the reader an explanation is coming.

These sentences are all about the Afterword. Some are right, and some hide a wrong sound-alike word. Tap every sentence that has a mistake. Then fix one, and explain why reading it out loud would never have caught the problem.

This is the last word work of the book, and it’s a full editing pass. Some sentences are already right. Some carry a wrong twin. Tap only what needs an editor, and leave the rest alone. Remember: your ear is no help here. Your eyes are.

Today’s Courage Watch is about ordinary people. My mother was not a hero in any book. She kept a neighbor family’s spare key in her sewing box for two years, and watered their plants until they came home. Lowry tells you Annemarie is made up. But people like my mother were real, all over Denmark. Read for them.

Now you write. Name one thing Lowry says is real and one thing she made up, using her own words. Then think about her friend who grew up in Copenhagen, and what that tells you about historical fiction. Last, set your essay’s claim beside what Lowry says about the Danish people, and publish.

The last four windows. When these words are in place, the whole street will be lit. You’ve met every one of these words before, so this is a chance to show yourself what you know. Shape, or bending? Then look up at the rooftops.

Read the Afterword slowly. Lowry talks to you directly here, one writer to one reader. She names what she made up and what really happened, and some of the true parts may surprise you. At the very end, she shares a letter from a real young man. Read his words twice.

This card belongs to Kim Malthe-Bruun. He was a young sailor who made secret trips across the water for the Resistance, until the Germans caught him. He was twenty-one. Lois Lowry saw his photograph and could not forget his eyes. She ends her whole book with words from his last letter. Read them slowly.

Same idea, word by word this time. Tap only the words that are the wrong twin. Then fix one and say the rule that helped you. If you made up a trick this week for remembering a pair, now is the time to use it.

One last match. Then use two of these words together, in a sentence about the whole book. Try compare and conclude: put the novel beside the real history, and say what you decide. Your sentence can be about Annemarie, about the real Danes, or about both at once.

Hello, this is Grete. The story is over, and now Lois Lowry steps out from behind it to speak to you herself. She tells you what was real. You’ll warm up, work with words, read the Afterword, and publish your essay. Today’s question: what in this novel actually happened, and what did the Danes really do?

Get out your list from this week, the one with could be real and made up. As you read the Afterword, check each guess against what Lowry actually says. Mark it real, made up, or still not sure. Then go back to one scene you loved, and read a few lines again, now that you know.
Conform. To fit in, to match a shape.
Transform. To change from one shape into another.
Reflect. To bend back, or to think back.
Flexible. Able to bend. And every window on the street is lit.

This is the day you publish. Paste in your whole finished essay. Then write three short sentences: what your claim was, what the real history says, and what putting them side by side taught you. Read it once more, out loud. You wrote an essay from the first idea to the last word.

A spare key in a sewing box. That's such a small way to say, we're waiting for you. In this way, every note is a letter. Start with Dear Ellen, and write to her like a best friend would, with I and you. And remember Grete's warning: Annemarie only knows what she saw or what someone told her. If she wasn't there, she can't tell it.

The safest secret looks dull. That's exactly why the soldiers missed so much. Every note in this way has two parts. On the outside tells what anyone would have seen. Really tells what it was doing. Before you write the Really part, check the chapter where the book explains it. Sometimes that's a few chapters later than you'd think.

Light coming back on, one window at a time. I love picturing that street. In this way, each window has its own speaker, so each note should sound like that person. Kirsti won't sound like Uncle Henrik. Each time you pick an object, choose whose window it is, and if that person didn't live to see the end of the war, let someone who loved them do the talking.

Let's look at what that note does. It says when: the night the soldiers came. It gives an exact detail: the star pressed its shape into her hand. And it says why: so the soldiers would believe Ellen was her sister. It sounds like Annemarie, too. Where, a detail, why, and the right voice. Your notes need all four.

Hear the two parts? On the outside, thin pages folded small. Really, a newspaper the Germans had banned. Then the note names the chapter and says why the secret mattered: someone could have been arrested. That last part is the one people forget. Don't just say what the secret was. Say why it had to stay hidden.

Notice who's talking in that one. It's Annemarie, remembering Peter, because Peter didn't live to see this night. The note is short, but every sentence is doing a job. It names the object, says where it came from, and says why she keeps it in the window. Yours can be three or four sentences. Make every one count.

A few things you could never throw away. I think everyone has a few of those. Before you choose, read all three ways, and open the model note under each one. Then ask yourself which one you can already picture. If you can see the box, or the street, or the secret, that's probably your way.

Mind your capitals, that’s what I always say. A lady’s title, her name, and the name of her village all deserve a capital letter. The sentence you’re fixing has forgotten every one of them, and it’s forgotten how to stop, besides. Study the correct one first. Ordinary words stay small. Proper names stand up straight. Everybody in Avonlea knows that.

Most words make more than one the sensible way. You add a letter and have done with it. But some words refuse to behave. One mouse, two mice. One goose, a whole yard of geese. You can’t reason those out. You simply have to know them, the way I know every family on this road. Sort them into two groups, and give each group a name of your own.

Words are a good deal like the families of Avonlea. Once you know who belongs with whom, everything makes sense. Today’s word parts both mean with, or together, and I know a thing or two about together. I run the Sewing Circle, I help with the Sunday-school, and I keep an eye on everybody else besides. Work through these carefully. I’ll be watching.

Open the book, and you’ll find me at my window. That’s where I do my best thinking. Now, I’m not one for imagination. I deal in plain facts. But when I saw Matthew Cuthbert drive off in his best suit, my mind went off in a dozen directions at once. Watch how much a person can imagine about a thing, just from looking out of a window.

Well. A boy from an orphan asylum, if you please. I told Marilla exactly what I thought of it, and I don’t take back a word. Now it’s your turn to say what you noticed. Don’t just tell me what happened. Point to the words in the book that show it. And mind you, the narrator may have noticed a thing or two about me as well.

Look at the start of a word before you look at the end of it. Every word today begins with a little part that means together. Conversation is my specialty, as anyone in Avonlea will tell you. It means turning words over together with a neighbor, and I can’t think of a better use of a spare hour. Spot that first part, and the long words stop looking so grand.

Here’s something I’ve noticed about plurals, and I notice a great deal. Most words simply add their letter and carry on. But a word that ends in a hissing sound needs an extra bit, or you’d never get your tongue round it. And a y at the end, with a consonant in front of it, has to change its ways. Sort them, then work out what makes the difference.

Four new words, and you’ll want them before the week is out. Placid means calm and still, like the brook by the time it reaches my house. It minds its manners there, you know. As for imagine, well, I’ve no great use for it myself. Plain sense serves me better. But try the three steps on every word, and see how close you get.

Hello, it’s Mrs. Rachel Lynde, and today I’ll be guiding you through your lesson. I live at the bottom of the hollow, and nothing in Avonlea gets past my window. Today’s question is how a writer makes a place feel real. By the end, you’ll be able to tell how the narrator describes Avonlea from how I see it. We’ll sort out some stubborn plurals, too.

Now, you’ll hear two voices telling you about me today. One is the narrator, who stands outside the story and sees everything. The other is me, and I’m generally right, of course. Keep the two of us apart as you read. When you meet a strong opinion, ask whose it is. You may find the narrator notices a thing or two about me that I’d never say myself.

You’re starting a story of your own, and every good story needs a question at the start of it. Mine was, where is Matthew Cuthbert going? I couldn’t rest until I knew. Give your character something they can’t leave alone. A worry, a wish, a mystery down the road. Then write your one sentence about who they are and what they’ll learn.

For the first question, go back and find the shouting. Copy two things exactly as they’re printed, one she did and one she said. For the second, find what Marilla said to me after the child went upstairs. Read it twice. It surprised me. For the third, you’ll need what the child told Marilla, because she certainly told me nothing. Look for her reasons.

You type every answer yourself today, so here’s my best advice. After each one, read the whole sentence back to yourself before you move on. You’ll catch half your own mistakes that way, I promise you. I always read a letter over twice before I send it. It’s saved me more embarrassment than I can tell you.

Here I am at Green Gables at last. Marilla says the child is out in the orchard. This week’s watch is about having a temper and having a reason. Here’s how to keep track of it. Whenever somebody gets upset, ask two things. What set them off? And were they right to be upset? You can say yes to that even if they behaved badly.

Well! I’ve never been so insulted in all my born days. I only said what anybody could see, that she’s skinny and homely with hair as red as carrots, and she flew at me, stamping and shouting. Marilla took her part, if you please. Now, answer these questions, and quote the book. I want proof, written down, of who was in the wrong.

Mrs. Rachel Lynde here, and I’ll keep you on track today, never fear. Today’s question is what makes a person’s faults easy to forgive, and what makes them hard to like. I see you’ll be tracking somebody’s temper. I can’t think whose. You’ll be typing possessive words yourself, too, apostrophes and all. Mind you read every sentence right to the end before you answer.

You’re to write one sentence about your character, showing something that belongs to them. Here’s how I’d choose. If they had to leave home in a hurry, what would they grab first? That’s theirs, and it tells you who they are. Put the owner’s name in front, with its apostrophe, and there’s your sentence. That child’s would be her temper, I expect.

I’ve lived in Avonlea all my life, and there isn’t a road or a pond I couldn’t name for you. That child put new names on half of them. The Lake of Shining Waters! It’s Barry’s pond, and always was. Still, I’ll grant you, she saw things in this place. Put your pins where things happened to her. I’d have done it in half the time, mind.

The first question asks for two things I do that Anne loves. I’d rather not guess at that myself, so look at what she tells Marilla. The second asks what the concert is for, and what parts Anne has. She has several, so count them all. The third asks why some grown-ups frown at my ways. They’re not wrong to be careful. Show both sides, in their own words.

The top sentence is a plain one, and every capital in it is earning its place. A title, a name, a day of the week. The bottom one is about my Friday afternoons, I think. It holds two thoughts, one that hasn’t happened yet and one that already has, and they’ve been run together. Find where the first one ends. Then look for every word that is somebody’s name, or a day’s.

Each sentence names a time in brackets, past or future, and your job is to make the doing word fit it. Some of these are about things Anne and Diana have already done, and you’ll recognize them. Be careful with the past ones. Not every doing word just adds an ending. A few change on the inside. Put yesterday in front and listen. Then type.

Today you build. You’ll type in a missing word part, fill in sentences, put a doing word into the time the bracket asks for, and add endings to words that end in y. Building is harder than spotting. When you spot, the answer is in front of you. When you build, it’s in you. Say each one aloud before you type. Your ear is a fine teacher. Better than me, some days.

There’s a box here about being called by your right name. I take some trouble over names. A child who hears her name said carelessly learns she doesn’t matter much, and that’s a hard lesson to unlearn. So I listen to how each pupil says her own, and I say it back the same way. It costs nothing at all. As you read, watch for a name that matters to somebody.

Now it’s your turn to write, and I’ll tell you what I tell my class. Don’t write what you think I want. Write what you noticed, and then show me where in the book you noticed it. A good answer points. If you can put your finger on the line, you’ve got it. If you can’t, go back and look. Some of the best compositions I get come from children who looked twice.

Four words, and each is missing its front. You know the two word parts by now. One means against, the other means away or down. Read the meaning after each blank first. Then ask which direction the meaning is pushing, against something, or away and down. Type the part that fits. On our field afternoons we look at a fern before we name it. Same here.

Two stops. The first comes early, when Anne talks about her new teacher. That’s me, so I’ll try not to listen. Think about why something so small could feel so large to her. The second comes once the concert is underway. Ask yourself what Anne wants most out of it. The acting, or being seen? You’ll have to decide. I’m not sure Anne knows herself.

That sentence is about me, which makes it rather awkward to read aloud. But look at how it’s put together. Two describing words up front, then with the happy gift of, and then what the person can do. It tells you what I’m like by what I do, not how I look. When you write yours, try the same. Pick someone you know, and name the thing they’re good at.

Three sentences, three blanks, and four words in the bank. So one word is left over, and that’s on purpose. Read every sentence through before you choose. Then say it aloud with your word in the blank. If it sounds like something a real person would say about a real person, you’ve likely got it. One of these sentences comes from today’s chapter. Listen for it later.

I’m Miss Stacy. Your question asks about the difference between a grown-up who notices you and one who doesn’t. I’m a teacher, so I had better have an answer, hadn’t I? Today the word work is mostly building, where you put the pieces together yourself. Then there’s a chapter about my schoolroom, and a concert. Keep an eye on who’s in the room.

The box says part of a setting is who’s there. A schoolroom full of children is a different place from the same room empty. Add a teacher who listens, and it changes again. Add an audience and a stage, and it changes again. So as you read, count who is in the room for each thing that happens. Then ask whether it would go the same way with different people there.

Today your kid has to do something. Not be rescued, not get lucky. Do. Anne in this chapter stops waiting and starts doing. She practices, she rehearses, she argues her case with Marilla. It doesn’t have to be grand. Getting up off the ground counts. Write the things your kid does, put a when word in front, and let somebody say one line. Then read it aloud.

The first question asks what my new class is for, and who joined it. Count them all, and notice who isn’t there. The second asks about Anne and Gilbert. I can tell you they work very hard to beat each other. The rest the book knows, and I don’t. The third asks you to look back over the whole week and choose one mistake.

The top sentence is about me, and I remember that day well. Look at what it does right. I count four things, and one of them is a comma doing a quiet job. Find all four before you tap. The bottom sentence runs two thoughts together. Find where the first one ends. Then look for a word that names a language. It wants a capital, and so does the girl.

A short draft, and some of the doing words are wrong. Not all of them. Tap only the ones a careful writer would fix, and leave the good ones alone. Say each sentence aloud and listen for the word that makes you wince. Then, in the box, tell me what the writer was reaching for. Mistakes usually make sense from the inside. That’s what makes them worth studying.

Review day, and two of these are traps. In the grammar and the spelling, some words are right and some are wrong, and tapping a right one costs you. So slow down. Read each word as if you were marking a composition. Then the vocabulary gives you a choice of what to write. Choose the one that will make you think hardest. That’s usually the one worth doing.

There’s a box here about learning from mistakes. I see a good many in a schoolroom, and I’ve come to think the mistake matters less than what happens after. When a pupil tells me the truth about one, I forgive it, and we don’t speak of it again. As you read, watch what Anne carries with her this year, and what she finds she has let go.

Now it’s your turn, and I’ll tell you what I tell my Queen’s class: don’t tell me, show me. For the first two questions, stay inside this chapter and put your finger on the line. The last one looks back across the whole week, and that takes a steadier hand. Anne would pick five mistakes and follow all of them. Pick one, and follow it to what it taught.

Matching once more. Two roots, two front parts, and four meanings to pair them with. You’ve had a week with these, so trust yourself. If one won’t come, think of a whole word with that part inside and say it aloud. On our field afternoons I never let anyone name a fern until they had looked at it properly. Look first, then tap.

One stop, at the very end. By then the year is over, and something has changed in Anne that I didn’t see. Nobody did, I think. Think about what it costs her, and why she keeps it to herself. Then think about what it tells you about how she’s growing up. You’ll know more about it than I do. That’s the privilege of a reader.

Six words, and some are spelled wrongly. Tap only those. For each one, ask whether the quiet e is doing its job. Is it there when the sound needs it? Is it missing when the next letter can do the work instead? Then, in the box, mend one and tell me what would happen to the sound without that e. Say it both ways. You’ll hear it.

The last day for this week’s four words, and you choose how to show you know them. You can write sentences, explain the parts, hunt for a word in today’s chapter that comes close, or teach one to someone younger. I like the teaching one best. You never really know a word until you’ve had to explain it to a small person with a great many questions.

I’m Miss Stacy. This chapter begins with a visit I paid to Green Gables, and it ends on the last day of a school year. Your question is about something Anne loses, and I’ll be honest, I can’t tell you what it is. A teacher sees a great deal, but not everything. First there’s word work, and some of it is already correct. Then read, and watch closely.

The box asks you to zoom out. Not one chapter, but the whole week, in two sentences. That means most of what happened has to go. I ask my older pupils to do the same with a year of history, and it hurts at first. Keep only what still matters at the end. If a moment changed nothing later, let it go, however much you enjoyed it.

Today, don’t fix anything. Read your whole story from the first line to the last, the way a stranger would. Then answer two questions. Which part is strongest, and which part still needs work? Name the scene. Name the sentence. Anne takes stock in this chapter of where she is and where she’s going. At the end of a year, so should a writer.

I had Anne in my class for two years, and I can tell you she didn’t change all at once. Nobody does. She changed in moments: a mistake, a quarrel, a kindness she didn’t expect. A real turning point has a before and an after. Look for the place where she stops and becomes a little different. You’ll know it when you find it.

You've just been thinking about the difference between the narrator's voice and a character's voice. Hold on to that. Today's chapter is called Mrs Rachel Lynde Is Surprised — and somebody in it is going to be very sure she is right. Before we get there, a little work on words. It's shorter than you think, and you're going to need it.

Now open the book. Chapter one is one woman at a window, watching a neighbor drive past in his good suit — and inventing a whole story about why. Watch that. This week we are following imagination, and Mrs Rachel shows you the cheap kind: imagining you already know. Somebody is coming who uses it the other way entirely.

So. Matthew drove past in his best suit, and Mrs Rachel could not let it go. Now you write about it. Don't rush to the answer you think somebody wants — say what you actually noticed, and point to the line that made you think it. And at the bottom, your own story is waiting. Today it's about voice, which is exactly what you just watched Montgomery do.

Same skill as yesterday. Narrator, and character. Chapter two has the same shape of title as chapter one — somebody else gets surprised. Watch who. First, though, words. You're still on the word parts that mean with, or together, and today they matter more than usual, because chapter two is about two people meeting who were not expecting each other at all.

Matthew goes to the station expecting a boy and finds a girl who does not stop talking. Listen to what she does on the drive home. A road under the trees, a pond, a view — Anne will not let any of them stay ordinary. Ask yourself why a girl with nothing of her own would want to give everything a name. And keep an eye on quiet Matthew while she does it.

Matthew went for a boy and came home with Anne, and said almost nothing the whole way. Now the questions. As you answer, think about how much you knew about Matthew even though he barely spoke. That is voice. And it is what you're building into your own character today — not a description. A way of being in the world.

Three chapters, three surprises. Mrs Rachel, then Matthew, and today Marilla. Montgomery is showing you one arrival through three different pairs of eyes, and asking you to notice that they don't agree. Keep that with you. First the word work — it's the same pattern you've been building all week, and today it should start to feel easy.

Two chapters today, and they pull in opposite directions. The first is an evening when Anne hears news she cannot imagine her way out of. The second is a morning at a window. Watch what her imagination does in each one. Does it rescue her, or can it not reach that far? The house stays exactly the same between the two chapters. Only Anne changes.

You've just watched Anne go from the worst evening of her life to a morning at a window, with the same house around her both times. That is the whole idea of perspective, in two chapters. Carry it into your answers. And carry it into your own story, where your character is starting to sound like somebody.

Here is today's question, and it is worth carrying with you: how does a writer make a place feel real — a place that only exists on paper? By the end of today you will be able to tell the difference between the way the narrator describes Avonlea and the way Mrs Rachel Lynde sees it. Those are not the same thing. You will also get to grips with some stubborn plurals — the ones that refuse to simply add an S.

Here is today's question, and it is a hard one. When somebody gets bad news, how does a writer show us how they feel — by telling us outright, or by letting us watch what they say and do? By the end of today you will be able to use the details on the page to explain how Anne takes the worst news of her life. Watch closely. It happens quickly.
companion
delight
imagine
placid
